name: John Paterakis Sr.
humbleBeginnings: Graduated from Patterson Park High School in 1947 and took over his father Steve's bakery, which started as a two-man operation working rented ovens on Fagley Street in Baltimore's Highlandtown.
breakthrough: Grew H&S Bakery into one of the largest bread, bun and roll producers in the U.S. Its Northeast Foods / Automatic Rolls division bakes buns for McDonald's from plants along the East Coast.
shieldingStrategy: Kept the company private with control concentrated in his hands, and recycled bakery cash flow into real estate. H&S Properties developed Baltimore's Harbor East waterfront.
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. The $1B+ tier is an estimate based on a 23-state private bakery business plus Harbor East, which Baltimore Magazine describes as ~$1B of development.

breakthroughDetail.t: Inherited a micro-bakery, scaled it nationally.
breakthroughDetail.d: H&S, named for brother-in-law Harry Tsakalos and father Steve, grew to operate in 23 states with ~2,000 employees.
Northeast Foods' Automatic Rolls plants (Baltimore, New Jersey, North Carolina, New England) produce McDonald's buns.
Redeployed operating cash flow into H&S Properties and the Harbor East district next to company headquarters.

shieldingDetail.d: "This company has one share of voting stock and that's me" (2013), so control stayed absolute and private.

shieldingDetail.t: Operating and property arms kept separate.
shieldingDetail.d: Bakery and real estate ran as distinct companies (H&S Bakery / H&S Properties), so risk in one didn't automatically reach the other.

After his death, a multimillion-dollar estate dispute between his widow and his children was settled in the children's favor (2021), a reminder that private structures still need clear succession documents.

sources.label: Baltimore Magazine — H&S Bakery chief John Paterakis Sr. dies at 87
NJBIZ — Northeast Foods, producer of McDonald's buns, expands
Baltimore Sun — Paterakis estate battle ends

name: A.G. Gaston
humbleBeginnings: Grandson of formerly enslaved people, born in Demopolis, Alabama. After Army service in World War I he worked in mines run by Tennessee Coal, Iron & Railroad near Birmingham, selling boxed lunches to fellow miners and lending them money at 25% interest.
breakthrough: Turned a miners' burial society into a Black-owned conglomerate: Booker T. Washington Insurance, Citizens Federal Savings & Loan, funeral homes, a business college, the Gaston Motel and Birmingham radio.
shieldingStrategy: Built community-chartered financial institutions (an insurer and an S&L) so Black enterprise capital didn't depend on banks that redlined it, then sold the companies to their employees to keep them Black-owned.

breakthroughDetail.d: Small weekly dues came in steadily and payouts came later. It was formalized as the Booker T. Washington Burial Society (1923) and later became an insurance company.
Owned funeral homes, so policy claims flowed back into his own operations.
Citizens Federal Savings & Loan (1957) lent to Black homeowners and businesses that white-owned banks refused.
Booker T. Washington Business College trained the clerks and agents his companies needed.

shieldingDetail.d: Housed 1963 Birmingham Campaign leaders at the Gaston Motel and helped post bail while publicly favoring negotiation, which kept white business counterparts at the table.
Sold his companies to employees at a fraction of market value rather than to outside acquirers.
Separately chartered, regulated companies limited how far any single legal, political or credit shock could spread.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — A. G. Gaston

name: Clarence Avant
humbleBeginnings: Born in Climax, North Carolina, the oldest of eight. He attended a one-room school through eighth grade, moved to New Jersey in 1947, and became manager of Teddy P's Lounge, a Newark nightclub.
breakthrough: Brokered record deals, label sales, endorsements and corporate mergers behind the scenes. His Venture Records (1967) was an early joint venture between a Black executive and a major label, and in 1973 he bought KAGB-FM, LA's first Black-owned FM station.
shieldingStrategy: Operated through privately held labels and stations (Venture Records, Sussex Records, Tabu Records, KAGB-FM) and avoided publicity. Most of his leverage was relationship capital rather than visible assets.
wealthNote: No reliable public net-worth figure exists. The tier is an estimate; he is included for the scale of deal flow he controlled.

breakthroughDetail.d: Went from negotiating for artists such as Little Willie John and Lalo Schifrin to owning labels: Venture, then Sussex (home of Bill Withers), then Tabu.
Bought KAGB-FM (formerly KTYM-FM, Inglewood) for $321,000 in 1973.
Became chairman of Motown's board in 1993 and was a trusted intermediary across music, sports and politics.
Tabu helped launch producers Jimmy Jam & Terry Lewis.

shieldingDetail.d: His role became widely known mainly through the 2019 Netflix documentary The Black Godfather.
Trust and favors can't be seized, sued away or assessed like property.
Specific fee and entity arrangements are not publicly documented.

sources.label: Hollywood Reporter — Clarence Avant dies at 92

name: Sheldon Lavin
humbleBeginnings: A Chicago financial consultant and former banker. In the early 1970s McDonald's wanted its family-run patty supplier, Otto & Sons, to build a dedicated plant, but the Ottos couldn't get financing.
breakthrough: Structured the plant financing in exchange for equity, took control as the family stepped back, and built OSI Group into a private global protein processor that follows McDonald's worldwide.
shieldingStrategy: Never took OSI public, so there are no proxy filings or outside shareholders, and its products ship under customers' brands, which leaves almost no consumer-facing name exposure.

breakthroughDetail.d: Became a partner rather than taking an advisory fee. The company was renamed OSI in 1975.
Built plants alongside McDonald's international expansion.
Expanded into poultry, pizza, bacon, vegetables and plant-based products for many customers.

shieldingDetail.d: Private ownership means minimal public disclosure.
White-label production keeps the name out of consumer view.

name: Louis Kuchuris
humbleBeginnings: Lost his father at age 6. In 1939 he bought Mary Ann, a bankrupt bakery on Chicago's northwest side that sold bread and buns to restaurants, drive-ins, hotels and schools.
breakthrough: A 1955 handshake with Ray Kroc to supply buns to Chicago-area McDonald's became East Balt, an automated bun bakery that grew to ~20 plants in 14 countries.
shieldingStrategy: Kept the business family-held for ~70 years, then exited through a private sale to JPMorgan's One Equity Partners (2012) rather than an IPO.
wealthNote: The family fortune was never published. The company later sold for ~$650M (One Equity Partners → Grupo Bimbo, 2017); that number measures the asset, not his personal wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Agreed with Ray Kroc to supply Chicago-area McDonald's from the chain's earliest days.
East Balt Commissary was an automated bun bakery dedicated to ~40 Chicago McDonald's.
Eventually supplied ~9,000 McDonald's worldwide.

shieldingDetail.d: Private from 1939 until the 2012 sale.
A private-equity sale turned a concentrated stake into cash without public-market disclosure.

sources.label: Baking Business — Baking Hall of Fame
Food Business News — East Balt sale to JPMorgan group
Bakery & Snacks — Grupo Bimbo buys East Balt

name: Chuck Feeney
humbleBeginnings: Born to a working-class Irish-American family in Elizabeth, New Jersey. He was an Air Force radio operator, studied at Cornell's hotel school on the GI Bill, then sold tax-free goods to U.S. servicemen in Europe.
breakthrough: Co-founded Duty Free Shoppers (1960), winning exclusive airport concessions just as Japanese outbound tourism surged.
shieldingStrategy: He created Atlantic Philanthropies in 1982 and in 1984 secretly and irrevocably transferred his entire 38.75% DFS stake to it, required grantees to keep the donor anonymous, and spent the foundation down to zero.

breakthroughDetail.d: Exclusive licenses at airport chokepoints gave pricing power without consumer brand-building.
Positioned DFS for the surge of Japanese travelers in Honolulu and Hong Kong.

shieldingDetail.d: His role surfaced only in 1997, when the sale of DFS to LVMH forced disclosure.
Atlantic spent down its endowment and closed instead of becoming a perpetual institution.

name: Jim Goodnight
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Wilmington, North Carolina, and worked on statistical software at NC State University as part of a federally funded agricultural research project.
breakthrough: Spun the NC State software into SAS Institute (1976) and licensed it on annual renewals, building recurring revenue decades before SaaS.
shieldingStrategy: Kept SAS private and venture-free for decades, with ownership concentrated between him and co-founder John Sall, so there were no outside shareholders or quarterly reporting.
wealthNote: Estimates move with private valuations of SAS. Check current figures and ownership status before publishing.

name: Reginald F. Lewis
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in East Baltimore, the son of a small-business owner and a teacher. As a boy he delivered the Baltimore Afro-American, built the route to 100 customers and sold it at a profit; he later went from Virginia State to Harvard Law School.
breakthrough: Left corporate law to found TLC Group in 1983. He bought McCall Pattern in a leveraged buyout for about $22.5M and sold it at a roughly 90-to-1 return, then in 1987 bought Beatrice International Foods (64 companies in 31 countries) for $985M. TLC Beatrice became the first Black-owned company with more than $1B in sales.
shieldingStrategy: Did his deals through a private partnership (TLC Group L.P.) that he controlled, using mostly borrowed money and very little equity. He moved wealth into the Reginald F. Lewis Foundation (1987), and after his death his widow Loida Nicolas Lewis took over running TLC Beatrice.

breakthroughDetail.d: McCall was bought with about $24M of borrowed cash and only $1M of equity. Lewis ended up with 81.7% of a roughly $90M payout.
Drexel Burnham Lambert and Michael Milken helped finance the $985M Beatrice International purchase in October 1987, the largest offshore leveraged buyout of its time.
TLC Beatrice reported $1.8B in revenue, making it the largest Black-owned business in the U.S.

shieldingDetail.d: TLC Group L.P. held his deals rather than a public holding company, so he didn't have to report to outside shareholders.
His widow Loida Nicolas Lewis took over as head of TLC Beatrice in 1994.
Set up the Reginald F. Lewis Foundation in 1987. His $3M gift to Harvard Law School (1992) was the school's largest from an individual at the time.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — The legacy of Reginald F. Lewis

name: John H. Johnson
humbleBeginnings: Born in Arkansas City, Arkansas. His family moved to Chicago in 1933 during the Great Migration, and he started as an office boy at Supreme Liberty Life Insurance under Harry Pace.
breakthrough: In 1942 his mother put up her furniture as collateral for a $500 loan, which paid for a mailing to 20,000 Supreme Life policyholders and launched Negro Digest. Ebony followed in 1945 and Jet in 1951, then Fashion Fair Cosmetics in 1973. In 1982 he became the first African American on the Forbes 400.
shieldingStrategy: Kept every business private and family-owned, never disclosed his personal holdings, and passed control to his daughter Linda Johnson Rice. In 1974 he also bought majority control of the insurer where he had started, Supreme Life.

breakthroughDetail.d: Used Supreme Life's own policyholder list to sell the first Negro Digest subscriptions: 3,000 subscribers at $2 each.
Ebony reached a peak circulation of 2.3 million, and Jet became the weekly news digest of Black America.
Launched Fashion Fair Cosmetics in 1973 after Estée Lauder and Revlon declined to partner with him.

shieldingDetail.d: All of his businesses were privately held, family-owned and family-operated, and he never disclosed his personal holdings.
Linda Johnson Rice became CEO in 2002 while he stayed on as chairman and publisher.
Served on the boards of Chrysler, Greyhound, Zenith, Continental Bank and Dillard's.

Ebony and Jet were sold in 2016, and Johnson Publishing filed for Chapter 7 in 2019. This suggests family control without outside capital protected ownership but not the business's long-term viability.

sources.label: EBSCO Research Starters — John H. Johnson

name: Herman J. Russell
wealthNote: Published estimates put his fortune at roughly $50M–$100M; a litigant's attorney argued the estate topped $100M. Much of it had already been moved to his children through trusts.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood and learned plastering from his father. At 12 he ran a shoeshine stand, and at 16 he bought a lot for $125 and built a duplex to pay for Tuskegee.
breakthrough: Built H.J. Russell & Company into the largest minority-owned real-estate and construction firm in the U.S., working on Atlanta–Fulton County Stadium, the Coca-Cola headquarters, Hartsfield-Jackson airport, the Georgia Dome and Turner Field. He also added airport food concessions (Concessions International) and sat on the Citizens Trust Bank board.
shieldingStrategy: Separated the group into distinct companies (construction, plastering, property management, airport concessions). Over decades he moved ownership to his three children through insurance trusts (1983), real-estate trusts (1993) and trusts holding majority control of the flagship and Concessions International (2013).

breakthroughDetail.d: Partnered with white-owned contractors on large public and private jobs, which built his reputation and his backlog.
Worked on Hartsfield-Jackson airport, the Georgia Dome, Philips Arena and Turner Field, and helped elect Maynard Jackson, Atlanta's first Black mayor, in 1973.
H.J. Russell & Company reported about $150M in sales by 1994.

shieldingDetail.d: Put about $5M of life insurance in trust for his children (1983) and $5M of real estate into trusts in their names (1993). In 2013 he moved majority control of the flagship and Concessions International into trusts seeded with $2.7M.
Most of his wealth passed outside probate through trusts, insurance and retirement accounts. This became contested after DNA showed he had a fourth child.
A friend of Martin Luther King Jr., he gave counsel and funding behind the scenes and became the first Black member of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Herman J. Russell
Atlanta Magazine — Russell estate and trusts

name: John W. Rogers Jr.
wealthNote: Forbes profiles him as self-made and says he owns about 34% of Ariel, which manages roughly $14B. A stake of that size in an asset manager that large is plausibly worth hundreds of millions; no Forbes figure was checked directly.
humbleBeginnings: Son of Chicago lawyer Jewel Lafontant and Tuskegee Airman John W. Rogers Sr. He captained Princeton's basketball team and worked as a broker at William Blair.
breakthrough: In 1983, at age 25, he founded Ariel Capital Management with about $10,000 from friends and family and built it on patient small- and mid-cap value investing. It became one of the largest Black-owned money managers in the U.S. at roughly $14B.
shieldingStrategy: Kept Ariel independent and insider-owned: employees and the board hold about 95%, with Rogers around 34% and co-CEO Mellody Hobson around 40%. He says he has never sold Ariel stock. He also built influence through boards such as McDonald's (2003–2023), Exelon, Aon and Nike.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built Ariel on a long-term value discipline. The Ariel Fund became the flagship product for retail investors.
Ariel Alternatives' Project Black raised $1.45B for middle-market investments with a focus on minority ownership.
On McDonald's board he pushed a $250M franchisee-diversity commitment and more spending with diverse suppliers.

shieldingDetail.d: Employees and the board own about 95% of Ariel. In 2019 Rogers moved shares to Hobson, the only time he has transferred his stock, to secure succession.
Holding his stake rather than selling to a larger asset manager kept Ariel independent and Black-owned.
Has sat on the boards of McDonald's, Exelon, Aon and Nike and been a University of Chicago trustee, giving him relationship capital beyond Ariel's balance sheet.

sources.label: Forbes profile — John W. Rogers Jr.
PR Newswire — Rogers retires from McDonald's board

name: Janice Bryant Howroyd
humbleBeginnings: The fourth of 11 children, born in Tarboro, North Carolina,. She moved to Los Angeles and started a staffing business in Beverly Hills in 1978 with about $1,500, including a $900 loan from her mother.
breakthrough: Built The ActOne Group into a global workforce-services group (staffing, background checks, HR tech and government contracting) with more than $1B in sales. She is often called the first Black woman to build a billion-dollar-revenue company.
shieldingStrategy: ActOne remains privately held and family-run; it is described as the largest privately held, minority-woman-owned personnel company. Separate subsidiaries for staffing, screening and government work spread its client and regulatory risk.

breakthroughDetail.d: Began with $1,500 and her mother's $900 loan instead of outside investors.
Grew to more than 17,000 clients and 2,600 employees in 33 countries.
As a certified minority- and woman-owned supplier, ActOne could win corporate and government supplier-diversity contracts.

shieldingDetail.d: No public float; Forbes counts the company as a family fortune.
Runs separate units such as ActOne Government Solutions, A-Check Global and DSSI under the group.
Treasurer of the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation and a trustee of North Carolina A&T.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Black women on Forbes' richest self-made women list

name: George E. Johnson Sr.
wealthNote: He controlled a public company with more than $31M in annual sales by 1974 and also founded a bank. No personal net-worth figure was published; the tier reflects the value of his controlling stake at peak.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Richton, Mississippi, and raised on Chicago's South Side. He shined shoes at eight, then sold door to door and worked in the lab at S.B. Fuller's Fuller Products.
breakthrough: Founded Johnson Products in 1954 with a $250 bank loan, which he got by telling the bank it was for a vacation. Ultra Sheen and Afro Sheen made it the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange (1971), and it was the first Black-controlled sponsor of Soul Train.
shieldingStrategy: Listed the company publicly while keeping family control, and in 1964 started his own bank, Independence Bank of Chicago, so Black businesses had access to credit. Control passed to his wife Joan in their 1989 divorce, and the company was sold to IVAX in 1993.

breakthroughDetail.d: Took a barber's hair-straightener idea that Fuller had turned down and refined it with a chemist into Ultra Wave, later Ultra Sheen.
Sponsored Soul Train and hired Black ad agencies (Vince Cullers, Burrell) for campaigns with positive Black imagery.
Became the first Black-owned company on the AMEX in 1971, with sales above $31M by 1974.

shieldingDetail.d: Founded Independence Bank of Chicago in 1964, giving Black businesses an alternative to banks that turned them away.
Joan Johnson took the controlling stake in the 1989 divorce, and the company was sold to Miami's IVAX in 1993, ending Black ownership.
Like A.G. Gaston, he started a chartered financial institution next to his operating company.

sources.label: Chicago Sun-Times — George E. Johnson dies at 99

name: Earl G. Graves Sr.
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. The estimate is based on private family ownership of Black Enterprise and his stake in the D.C. Pepsi franchise, bought in a $60M deal with Magic Johnson (1990) and sold to Pepsi (1998).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Brooklyn's Bedford-Stuyvesant to immigrants from Barbados and Trinidad. He studied economics at Morgan State and later worked as an aide to Senator Robert F. Kennedy.
breakthrough: Launched Black Enterprise in August 1970 as a business magazine for Black entrepreneurs. Its BE 100s rankings made it the official scorekeeper of Black business. In 1990 he and Magic Johnson bought the Pepsi-Cola bottling franchise for Washington, D.C., and Graves ran it as CEO until 1998.
shieldingStrategy: Held everything through a private holding company, Earl G. Graves Ltd., covering publishing, events, radio and TV. He sold the bottling stake back to Pepsi in 1998 and kept Black Enterprise in the family under his son Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr.

breakthroughDetail.d: The BE 100s list and Company of the Year awards (to TLC Beatrice in 1988 and Barden Cos. in 2003, for example) made Black Enterprise the central record of Black business.
Bought and ran the Pepsi bottler for the nation's capital with Magic Johnson from 1990 to 1998, a supply-chain franchise rather than a media asset.
Sat on the boards of Aetna, AMR (American Airlines), Daimler, Federated Department Stores and Rohm and Haas.

shieldingDetail.d: Earl G. Graves Ltd. owned the magazine and its related publishing, event, radio and TV divisions.
Sold the bottling stake back to the franchisor, PepsiCo, in 1998.
His son Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr. became president and CEO of Black Enterprise.

sources.label: NBC News — Earl Graves championed Black business
Black Enterprise — The legacy of Reginald F. Lewis

name: Percy Sutton
wealthNote: No published personal figure. Inner City Broadcasting had about $59M in revenue at its peak, and its stations later sold for $180M (2012), though under heavy debt.
humbleBeginnings: Youngest of 15 children, born in San Antonio, Texas. He stowed away to New York at 12, served as a Tuskegee Airmen intelligence officer, and worked as a lawyer, including as Malcolm X's attorney.
breakthrough: While serving as Manhattan Borough President (1966–77) he co-founded Inner City Broadcasting (1970–71), which bought WLIB in 1972 and WBLS-FM in 1974 and then added stations in other cities. In 1981 Inner City bought the Apollo Theater at a bankruptcy sale for $225,000, renovated it and produced It's Showtime at the Apollo.
shieldingStrategy: Pooled capital from more than 50 Black shareholders, including Hal Jackson, David Dinkins, Betty Shabazz and Roberta Flack, through one private broadcasting company, then extended it into a venue and TV production.

breakthroughDetail.d: WBLS FM became the city's first African American-owned radio station.
Bought the Apollo out of bankruptcy, put in $250K of his own money and arranged about $18M for renovation, including a TV studio that produced It's Showtime at the Apollo (from 1987).
Inner City grew to stations in Los Angeles, Detroit, San Francisco, Philadelphia and Jackson, Mississippi.

shieldingDetail.d: More than 50 prominent Black New Yorkers held shares, spreading the capital and political cover.
Creditors forced the company into Chapter 11 in 2011, and YMF Media bought 15 stations for $180M in 2012.
He held elected office and built the company at the same time, a combination rare among his peers.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Showdown at the Apollo

name: Comer Cottrell
wealthNote: Pro-Line sold to Alberto-Culver for a reported $75M–$80M in 2000; he co-owned it with his brother. He also turned a $500K Texas Rangers stake into about $3M.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Mobile, Alabama, he left the University of Detroit and served in the Air Force during the Korean War. He and his brother James started Pro-Line in Los Angeles in 1970 with $600 and a broken typewriter.
breakthrough: Pro-Line's Curly Kit (1979) brought the salon-only Jheri curl to drugstores for about $8 a box. Forbes called it the biggest single product ever in the Black cosmetics market. He moved the company to Dallas in 1980.
shieldingStrategy: Kept Pro-Line private and brother-owned until he sold it to Alberto-Culver in 2000. He diversified into a minority stake in the Texas Rangers (1989–98, alongside George W. Bush) and bought the Bishop College campus, which became Paul Quinn College's new home.

breakthroughDetail.d: Packaged an expensive salon process as an affordable at-home kit.
$600 of capital and a family partnership with his brother James.
Moved to Dallas in 1980, where he became the first Black member of the Dallas Citizens Council.

shieldingDetail.d: Pro-Line stayed in the brothers' hands until the sale.
Put $500K into the Bush-led Texas Rangers group and made about $3M when the team was sold.
Took cash from a large consumer-products company instead of going public.

name: Don H. Barden
wealthNote: He personally received about $105M when he sold his Detroit cable system to Comcast in 1994, and by 2003 he wholly owned a casino group with $347M in revenue. Bankruptcies after 2009 reduced his fortune later.
humbleBeginnings: The ninth of 13 children, raised on a nine-acre farm in Inkster, Michigan. He opened a record shop in Lorain, Ohio, in 1966 with $500 of savings, then started a newspaper and a PR firm.
breakthrough: Won the Detroit cable franchise through Barden Communications/Barden Cablevision and built one of the largest urban cable systems in the U.S. He sold it to Comcast in 1994 and put the money into gaming, starting with the Majestic Star riverboat in Gary. In 2001 he bought three Fitzgeralds casinos, becoming the first Black casino owner in Las Vegas.
shieldingStrategy: Held everything in a privately owned holding company, Barden Companies, with the casinos in a separate LLC (Majestic Star Casino) financed mostly with bonds: $14M of his own money and $135M of bonds for Fitzgeralds. When Majestic Star went bankrupt in 2009, the losses stayed inside that entity.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built wealth on government-granted franchises: a city cable franchise, then state gaming licenses.
Moved his Comcast proceeds straight into the Majestic Star and then the Fitzgeralds purchase.
Barden International contracted to convert GM vehicles in Namibia. In 1998 he partnered with Michael Jackson on a proposed Detroit casino and theme park, which failed.

shieldingDetail.d: Barden Companies held separately financed subsidiaries for casinos, real estate and international work.
Most of the casino purchase money was the bondholders', not his, which limited how much of his personal capital was at risk.
Majestic Star and the Fitzgeralds casinos filed in November 2009 and the properties went to creditors in 2011.

sources.label: Reference for Business — Barden Companies history
ClickOnDetroit — Casino magnate Don Barden dies

name: S.B. Fuller
wealthNote: His company peaked at about $18M in annual sales in the 1950s, and he also owned newspapers, a theater and a department store. No exact personal figure was published.
humbleBeginnings: Born to sharecroppers in Monroe, Louisiana, he left school after sixth grade and was selling door to door by age nine. He moved to Chicago in 1928.
breakthrough: Started Fuller Products with $25 borrowed against his car, selling soap door to door, and grew it to about 5,000 salespeople. In 1947 he secretly bought Boyer International Laboratories, a white-owned cosmetics maker, and he later bought the Pittsburgh Courier, New York Age, the Regal Theater and a department store.
shieldingStrategy: Kept his ownership of Boyer hidden so white customers wouldn't boycott it, and ran his holdings as separate companies (Fuller Products, Fuller Guaranty Corp., the Courier newspaper group, the Regal Theater). Separate entities couldn't prevent a 1968 SEC case over unregistered promissory notes and a 1971 bankruptcy.

breakthroughDetail.d: A door-to-door army of about 5,000 salespeople reached $18M in sales in the 1950s.
Bought Boyer International Laboratories in 1947 without disclosing that the buyer was Black.
John H. Johnson and George E. Johnson both gained business experience in his orbit; George Johnson worked in Fuller's lab.

shieldingDetail.d: White consumers boycotted Boyer products once his ownership became known in the 1960s.
Kept separate companies for products, finance (Fuller Guaranty), media and real estate.
The SEC charged him in 1968 over unregistered promissory notes he used to raise money; he went bankrupt in 1971, then returned to a $300K annual profit.

name: Madam C.J. Walker
wealthNote: Wikipedia puts her estate at $500K–$1M in 1919, roughly $9M–$18M in today's dollars. The tier uses that inflation-adjusted figure.
humbleBeginnings: Born Sarah Breedlove in Delta, Louisiana, to formerly enslaved parents. She was orphaned at seven and worked as a laundress earning little more than a dollar a day.
breakthrough: Worked as a commission agent for Annie Turnbo Malone's Poro Company, then launched her own hair-care line in Denver (1905–06). She built the Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis (1910) with thousands of trained sales agents.
shieldingStrategy: Kept the company wholly in the family, with her daughter A'Lelia as successor president. Her will sent two-thirds of the estate's future net profits to charity and left nearly $100,000 to institutions.

breakthroughDetail.d: Employed several thousand women as sales agents between 1911 and 1919 and claimed to have trained nearly 20,000 by 1917.
Opened an Indianapolis headquarters and factory in 1910.
Picked up Poro's agent-sales system before starting her own competing brand.

shieldingDetail.d: Her will directed two-thirds of future net profits to charity.
A'Lelia Walker succeeded her as president.
Her $5,000 anti-lynching pledge was the largest individual gift the NAACP had received.

name: Annie Turnbo Malone
wealthNote: Described as a multimillionaire by the 1920s; she paid nearly $40,000 in income tax in 1924, reportedly the highest in Missouri. Even $1M in the 1920s is more than $15M in today's dollars.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Metropolis, Illinois, to formerly enslaved parents. She was orphaned young and raised by older siblings, and developed an early interest in chemistry and her own hair formulas.
breakthrough: Made and sold 'Wonderful Hair Grower' and opened a St. Louis shop in 1902. In 1918 she opened Poro College, a combined cosmetology school, factory and retail hub that created work for about 75,000 women agents.
shieldingStrategy: Copyrighted the Poro brand to protect it from imitators, including her former agent Sarah Breedlove (Madam C.J. Walker). When her 1927 divorce put Poro into receivership, she paid a $200,000 settlement to her husband to keep sole ownership.

breakthroughDetail.d: Poro College trained the agents who sold her products.
Copyrighted the Poro name after Walker left to start a competing line.
Created jobs for about 75,000 women across several continents.

shieldingDetail.d: Paid a $200,000 settlement to keep sole ownership after the 1927 divorce and receivership.
Moved operations to Chicago's South Parkway.
Gave to Howard University's medical school and the YMCA, and ran the board of the St. Louis Colored Orphans Home (1919–1943).

name: Alonzo Herndon
wealthNote: Known as Atlanta's first Black millionaire. Real estate alone was valued at nearly $325,000 at his death in 1927, plus control of Atlanta Life. $1M in 1927 is roughly $18M today.
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in 1858 in Walton County, Georgia, to an enslaved mother and a white father. He left Social Circle in 1878 with little formal schooling and learned barbering.
breakthrough: Ran three upscale Atlanta barbershops, including a chandeliered shop at 66 Peachtree that served white judges and politicians. In 1905 he bought a failing mutual-aid association and built it into Atlanta Life Insurance, one of five Black insurers with legal-reserve status by 1922.
shieldingStrategy: Turned a mutual-aid society into a legal-reserve life insurer that he controlled and put his barbershop profits into real estate. After his death his son Norris and widow Jessie held control as major stockholders and directors.

breakthroughDetail.d: Barbershops serving Atlanta's white elite produced cash and connections.
Bought a failing mutual-aid society in 1905 and incorporated it as Atlanta Mutual Insurance Association.
The 1922 reorganization as Atlanta Life put it among only five Black insurers with legal-reserve status.

shieldingDetail.d: Held nearly $325,000 of property at his death.
His son Norris succeeded him as CEO, and Norris and Jessie Herndon held control as major stockholders.
His businesses were targeted in the 1906 Atlanta race massacre, and barbers across the street from his shop were killed.

name: Maggie Lena Walker
wealthNote: An analysis of her will cited by a secondary source puts her net worth at about $45,000 in 1934, roughly $900,000 in today's dollars. The analyst isn't named, so treat this as approximate.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Richmond, Virginia, in 1864. After her stepfather died, her mother supported the family as a laundress, and young Maggie delivered the clean clothes while attending segregated schools.
breakthrough: Joined the Independent Order of St. Luke, a mutual-aid society, at 14 and became its Right Worthy Grand Secretary in 1899, rescuing it from near collapse. In 1903 she chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank, becoming the first African American woman to charter a U.S. bank.
shieldingStrategy: Grew wealth for the community rather than herself. The fraternal order collected dues and fed deposits to its own bank. In 1930 she merged the bank with two others into Consolidated Bank and Trust, which survived the Depression and stayed Black-owned until 2005.

breakthroughDetail.d: The Order collected nearly $3.5 million during her 25 years and claimed 100,000 members in 24 states.
The bank opened in November 1903 with 280 deposits totaling $8,340.44, and handed out penny banks to children. By 1920 it had helped 645 Black families pay off their homes.
The St. Luke Herald (1902) became Richmond's most popular Black weekly.

shieldingDetail.d: Merged St. Luke with Second Street Savings Bank and another bank into Consolidated Bank and Trust in 1930, and chaired it until her death.
She drew a $25-a-week salary as bank president. The wealth stayed in the institutions, not in her own estate.
The St. Luke Emporium department store (1905) faced organized opposition from white merchants and closed in 1911.

sources.label: NPS — The St. Luke Penny Savings Bank
The New La Villa — Lost Fortunes: Maggie Lena Walker (estate analysis)

name: Robert Reed Church Sr.
wealthNote: Widely described as the South's first African American millionaire, collecting about $6,000 a month in rent. $1M around 1912 is roughly $30M in today's dollars.
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in 1839 in Holly Springs, Mississippi, the son of a white steamboat owner and an enslaved woman. After his mother died he worked as steward of a steamboat's mess hall on the Memphis–New Orleans run.
breakthrough: During the 1878 yellow-fever epidemic, which killed more than 5,000 people in Memphis, he bought property at depressed prices. He built a real-estate empire, along with a saloon, restaurant and hotel, and in 1906 founded Solvent Savings Bank, the first Black-owned bank in Memphis.
shieldingStrategy: Kept his wealth in rental real estate and in a bank he controlled. To stop a run in the 1907 panic, he put bags of money in the bank's windows. His son Robert Church Jr. succeeded him as bank president in 1912.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bought devalued Memphis property during and after the 1878 epidemic.
Estimated to collect about $6,000 a month in rents later in life.
Solvent Savings became the first African American-owned bank to reach $1 million in assets.

shieldingDetail.d: Put bags of cash in the bank's windows in the 1907 panic to show depositors their money was safe.
Church's Park and Auditorium (valued at $100,000 when built) was a venue Black Memphians controlled; Theodore Roosevelt spoke there in 1902.
His son ran the bank from 1912. After an October 1927 merger with Fraternal Savings, the combined bank collapsed, and about 28,000 depositors lost roughly 90% of their savings.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Solvent Savings Bank and Trust
African American Registry — Robert Reed Church Sr.

name: Anthony Overton
wealthNote: Described as a self-made millionaire; his cosmetics company alone was valued at more than $1 million. $1M in the 1920s is roughly $15–18M in today's dollars.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Monroe, Louisiana, in 1865 to a father who had been enslaved. He studied chemistry at Washburn College and law at the University of Kansas, and briefly served as a judge in Kansas.
breakthrough: Founded the Hygienic Manufacturing Company in 1898. Its High-Brown Face Powder was the first market success in cosmetics made for Black women. After moving to Chicago in 1911 he added Half-Century Magazine, Douglass National Bank, Victory Life Insurance, Great Northern Realty and the Chicago Bee.
shieldingStrategy: Built a conglomerate of separately chartered companies: a manufacturer, a national bank, an insurer, a realty company and a newspaper, all in his own Overton Hygienic Building in Bronzeville. During the Depression the bank and insurer ran into trouble, with mismanagement at both.

breakthroughDetail.d: High-Brown Face Powder was advertised as the first face powder made especially for Black women's complexions.
Douglass National Bank was the second nationally chartered Black-owned bank in the U.S.
In 1927 he received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal and the first Harmon Gold Medal for business.

shieldingDetail.d: The four-story Overton Hygienic Building (1923, 3619 S. State St.) housed manufacturing and offices.
The cosmetics maker outlived the failed bank and insurer and kept operating until 1983.
The financial units shared management and fell into trouble together during the Depression.

name: Jesse Binga
wealthNote: His wife Eudora inherited about $200,000 in 1907, roughly $6.5M today, and by the 1920s he held about 1,200 property leaseholds plus control of a bank with more than $1M in deposits. Everything was lost after 1930.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Detroit in 1865, the youngest of ten children of a barber. He helped his mother collect rents, then traveled west and arrived in Chicago in 1893 with about $10, starting out as a fruit peddler.
breakthrough: Bought run-down South Side buildings, renovated them and rented them to Great Migration arrivals. He grew to about 1,200 leaseholds and in 1908 opened the first Black-owned bank in the North, chartered as Binga State Bank in 1921, with the Binga Arcade next door.
shieldingStrategy: Married Eudora Johnson, heir to gambling boss John 'Mushmouth' Johnson's fortune, and held his wealth in real estate and his own bank. The real estate was concentrated in one area and the bank had a single owner, so when it became the first Chicago bank to fail in the Depression (1930) he lost everything. He was convicted of embezzlement and later pardoned (1941).

breakthroughDetail.d: Rented renovated buildings to Black migrants at premium prices.
Opened a private bank in 1908, got a state charter in 1921, and by 1924 had more than $1M in deposits.
Eudora Johnson's 1907 inheritance of about $200,000 added to the couple's base.

shieldingDetail.d: Real estate and the bank were tied to the same neighborhood and the same owner.
The bank closed in June 1930. Binga was convicted of embezzlement in 1933, paroled in 1938, pardoned in 1941, and died in poverty.
His home in a white neighborhood was bombed at least five times.

sources.label: Beverly Area Planning Association — Jesse Binga

name: Robert S. Abbott
wealthNote: Described as one of the first self-made African American millionaires. $1M in the 1920s is roughly $15–18M in today's dollars.
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1870 on St. Simons Island, Georgia, to formerly enslaved parents; his father died when he was a baby. He learned printing at Hampton Institute and earned a law degree, but racial prejudice kept him from practicing.
breakthrough: Founded the Chicago Defender in 1905 with 25 cents, working out of his boarding-house room. Circulation passed 200,000 by the early 1920s, about two-thirds of it outside Chicago, and the paper's 'Great Northern Drive' (May 15, 1917) helped drive the Great Migration.
shieldingStrategy: Kept the Defender wholly owned and left it by will to his nephew John H. Sengstacke, who built it into a chain that added the Michigan Chronicle, the Tri-State Defender and the New Pittsburgh Courier. The family held it until 2003.

breakthroughDetail.d: Started with 25 cents and a rented room.
Circulation went from 50,000 (1916) to 125,000 (1918) to more than 200,000 (early 1920s).
Promoted northern migration, which in turn grew the Defender's own Chicago readership.

shieldingDetail.d: Willed the paper to his nephew John H. Sengstacke.
Sengstacke bought the Pittsburgh Courier in the 1960s and relaunched it as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967.
The chain was sold to Real Times in 2003.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Robert Sengstacke Abbott
PBS The Black Press — Robert Abbott

name: James Forten
wealthNote: Estimated at more than $100,000 by the early 1830s, about $3M in today's dollars. That made him one of the wealthiest Philadelphians of any race.
humbleBeginnings: Born free in Philadelphia in 1766, the son of a sailmaker. At 14 he served on the privateer Royal Louis and was captured by the British; he refused an offer of education in England.
breakthrough: Apprenticed in 1790 to sailmaker Robert Bridges, his father's old employer, and bought the sail loft when Bridges retired in 1798. His sail-handling innovations made it one of the most successful lofts in Philadelphia.
shieldingStrategy: Moved sail-loft profits into real estate and bank and canal stocks, diversifying away from the shipping cycle. He kept a racially integrated workforce and spent much of his fortune funding William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator.

breakthroughDetail.d: Made sails for Philadelphia shipowners, a classic B2B supply position.
Rose from apprentice to foreman to owner of his mentor's shop.
Employed both Black and white workers at one of Philadelphia's largest lofts.

shieldingDetail.d: Put profits into real estate and bank and canal stocks.
Bankrolled The Liberator and wrote for it as 'A Colored Man of Philadelphia.'
His daughters married into leading abolitionist families.

name: Bridget "Biddy" Mason
wealthNote: Accumulated nearly $300,000, which the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center puts at about $10M in today's dollars.
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in 1818 in Hancock County, Georgia. She walked behind her enslaver's Mormon wagon train to Utah (1848) and San Bernardino, California (1851), and won her family's freedom in a Los Angeles court in 1856.
breakthrough: Worked as a midwife and nurse and in 1866 paid $250 for a lot on Spring Street, which became the heart of downtown Los Angeles' financial district. She bought and sold more lots as the city grew.
shieldingStrategy: Held her savings in downtown land rather than cash, and sold parcels selectively (for example, half the Spring Street lot for $1,500 in 1875). Her family kept the property; her grandson Robert C. Owens became the wealthiest Black man in Los Angeles.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bought on Spring Street for $250 in 1866, before the city's boom.
Sold half the Spring Street lot for $1,500 (1875) and an Olive Street lot for $2,800 (1884).
Her midwifery and nursing gave her steady income and community standing.

shieldingDetail.d: Downtown lots appreciated as Los Angeles grew.
Her grandson Robert Curry Owens became known as the wealthiest Black man in Los Angeles.
With her son-in-law Charles Owens she founded and financed Los Angeles' First AME Church in 1872, the city's first Black church.

sources.label: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center — Biddy Mason

name: Thomy Lafon
wealthNote: Worth an estimated $250,000 in 1870, and left about $500,000 to charities in 1893, roughly $17M in today's dollars. He was considered the wealthiest Black man in the U.S. when he died.
humbleBeginnings: Born free in New Orleans around 1810 as a Creole of color. He started out selling cakes to workers and running a small dry-goods business.
breakthrough: Became a moneylender and real-estate investor in French-speaking New Orleans, buying heavily from 1868 onward. By 1870 his estimated $250,000 made him the wealthiest African American in the country.
shieldingStrategy: Lived modestly and kept his fortune in real estate and loans. His will left most of it to New Orleans institutions, including Charity Hospital, the Sisters of the Holy Family, the Lafon Old Folks' Home and Straight University.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built his wealth through moneylending and real-estate investment.
Bought real estate heavily starting in 1868.
Considered the wealthiest Black man in the U.S. at his death.

shieldingDetail.d: Kept personal spending low while growing his capital.
His bequest to Charity Hospital alone was about $25,600.
The Thomy Lafon School (1897) and the Lafon homes carried his name.

sources.label: Abandoned Southeast — Lafon Home for Boys

name: Jeremiah G. Hamilton
wealthNote: Historian Shane White puts his fortune at about $2 million in 1875, which sources call a quarter of a billion in today's money. A straight CPI adjustment gives roughly $55–60M, so the tier uses the more conservative figure.
humbleBeginnings: His origins are deliberately obscure. Contemporary accounts say he was born in Virginia to free parents, while his death certificate says the West Indies. In 1828 he was caught up in a scheme shipping counterfeit coins to Haiti and was sentenced to death there in absentia.
breakthrough: Became a Wall Street broker and speculator in New York, profiting from property bought after the 1835 Great Fire, Hudson River land and railway stocks. Contemporaries called him the only Black millionaire in New York.
shieldingStrategy: Worked as an independent trader and used lawsuits aggressively to defend his positions, filing countless suits. He took on Cornelius Vanderbilt's Accessory Transit Company in the 1850s and was remembered as the man who fought the Commodore.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bought Manhattan property after the 1835 Great Fire of New York.
Traded aggressively on Wall Street and filed countless lawsuits to back his positions.
Owned shares in railways that refused to carry Black passengers.

shieldingDetail.d: Defended his trades and property with constant lawsuits.
No portrait or photograph of him is known to survive, and his origins stayed murky.
Vanderbilt's obituary named him as the only man who ever fought the Commodore.

sources.label: AHA Perspectives — Wall Street's First Black Millionaire (review of Prince of Darkness)

name: Robert Warren Miller
humbleBeginnings: Born in Quincy, Massachusetts in 1933 and graduated from Cornell's hotel school in 1955. He drifted through the U.S. and Mexico, sailed to Spain in 1957 and worked at Barcelona's Ritz Hotel, where he reconnected with fellow Cornellian Chuck Feeney.
breakthrough: With Feeney he founded Duty Free Shoppers in 1960, first selling tax-free liquor to U.S. servicemen. The business was rescued by the 1962 Honolulu and Hong Kong airport concessions, which boomed when Japanese outbound tourism took off after the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
shieldingStrategy: Refused to sell when his partners took LVMH's 1996 offer, and kept roughly 38% of DFS as the only founder still in the business. After the 1986 U.S. tax changes the DFS partners held their stakes through tax shelters and foundations rather than in their own names.

breakthroughDetail.d: When the servicemen business fell apart in 1965, Miller wound it down over 1965-67 and kept the company alive on cash from the Honolulu and Hong Kong airport stores.
DFS expanded to Anchorage, San Francisco, Guam, Saipan, Sydney and New Zealand by bidding for exclusive airport licences.
From 1977 to 1995 the founders split about 90% of annual profits, an estimated $3 billion in total.

shieldingDetail.d: Miller opposed the 1996 LVMH deal and went to arbitration. When LVMH would not negotiate further, he stayed on as a ~38% minority partner rather than selling.
After the 1986 tax overhaul the partners became 'shareholder representatives of tax shelters and charitable foundations' rather than direct owners.
He founded Search Investment Group in 1973 to hold assets outside DFS.

His daughters married Christopher Getty, Crown Prince Pavlos of Greece and Alexander von Fürstenberg (Pia and Alexandra have since divorced). The marriages tied the fortune socially to old money but did not merge it with theirs.

sources.label: Moodie Davitt Report - The Moodie Interview: DFS founder Bob Miller
Wikipedia - Marie-Chantal, Crown Princess of Greece

name: Alan M. Parker
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1939 in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe), the son of a British colonial civil servant. He trained as an accountant.
breakthrough: Brought into Duty Free Shoppers in 1966 with a 10% stake to help restructure the company. He later held about 20%, and sided with Feeney to sell it to LVMH in 1996-97 for roughly $840 million.
shieldingStrategy: Turned his DFS proceeds into diversified investments, including hedge funds and technology, from a base in Geneva. In 1983 he created the Oak Foundation, a large and fairly low-profile private grant-maker.

breakthroughDetail.d: Feeney and Miller gave Parker and lawyer Tony Pilaro 10% each in 1966 to restructure the company.

breakthroughDetail.t: Swing vote in the LVMH sale.
breakthroughDetail.d: Feeney's and Parker's holdings together made up 58.75%, enough to sell control to LVMH over Miller's objection after arbitration.
He got about $840 million for his ~20% stake. By 2014 his fortune was estimated at £2.34B.

shieldingDetail.d: He founded the Oak Foundation in Geneva in 1983, the year after Feeney set up Atlantic. It reported about $383 million in grants across 33 countries in 2025.
He moved the proceeds into hedge funds and technology ventures instead of keeping a stake in one operating company.
Both partners put DFS wealth into private foundations in the early 1980s. Parker kept a personal fortune; Feeney did not.

name: Anthony M. Pilaro
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. He was paid $105 million for his remaining 2.5% of DFS in 1997, after three decades of DFS dividends on a stake that started at 10%. His family vehicles also held about 44.5% of BriteSmile.
humbleBeginnings: Studied at the University of Virginia (BA 1957, law 1960) and practised as a tax lawyer in New York until 1964.
breakthrough: Brought into Duty Free Shoppers in 1966 with a 10% stake to restructure the company. He brokered a financing deal with Butlers Bank of Nassau that let DFS get out of the car-import business, then served as chairman (1966-75) and CEO (1972-75).
shieldingStrategy: Ran his wealth through a Dublin family office, CAP Advisers. It acted as co-trustee of the ERSE Trust, which wholly owned LCO Investments, BriteSmile's main shareholder. He formally disclaimed beneficial ownership of shares held by those trusts and by his charitable foundation.

breakthroughDetail.d: He got 10% of DFS in 1966 for restructuring work, including the Butlers Bank of Nassau financing.
He first sided with Miller against LVMH, then sold his 2.5% in January 1997 for $105 million.
Founder of the predecessor of VISX (laser vision correction) and chairman of BriteSmile (tooth whitening).

shieldingDetail.d: SEC filings show BriteSmile's main holder, LCO Investments, was wholly owned by the ERSE Trust, with Pilaro's CAP Advisers as co-trustee and family office.
Filings list several family trusts (AMP, LCP II, ACP II, CAP II) and the CAP Charitable Foundation, all of whose shares he disclaimed.
He founded the Ron Brown Scholar Program in 1996 and funded UVA's Jerome Holland and Hardy Dillard scholarships.

sources.label: Ron Brown Scholar Program - Anthony M. Pilaro

name: Vichai Srivaddhanaprabha
humbleBeginnings: Born Vichai Raksriaksorn in Bangkok in 1958 into a Chinese-Thai family with roots in Fujian. He studied at Ramkhamhaeng University and Northrop University, and began his career in the duty-free department of the Tourism Authority of Thailand.
breakthrough: In 1989 he partnered with Hong Kong-based DFS to open Downtown DFS (Thailand), the country's first downtown duty-free shop. He formed King Power International in 1994, won Don Mueang Airport's duty-free concession in 1995, and then held all duty-free space at Suvarnabhumi from its 2006 opening, a 16-year monopoly.
shieldingStrategy: Kept King Power private and family-controlled. Leicester City was bought through a separate consortium, Asia Football Investments, and King Power took a 39% stake in Thai AirAsia. Control passed to his son Aiyawatt after his 2018 death.

breakthroughDetail.d: His first duty-free venture, Downtown DFS (Thailand) at Mahatun Plaza (1989), was a partnership with Duty Free Shoppers. Goods bought downtown were collected at the airport.
He won the Don Mueang concession in 1995 and Suvarnabhumi in 2004 (opened 2006, extended to 2020). Wikipedia notes that provincial airport concessions were awarded without bidding.
He bought Leicester City (2010; Premier League champions 2016), 39% of Thai AirAsia for $226M (2016) and the MahaNakhon tower.

shieldingDetail.d: King Power never listed, so concession profits stayed inside a family-held group.
Leicester City was bought through the Asia Football Investments consortium with his son Aiyawatt, not by King Power directly.
In 2012 King Bhumibol granted the family the surname Srivaddhanaprabha, and King Power received a royal warrant in 2009.

sources.label: Asia Times - Thailand's duty-free monopoly up for grabs (2019)
The Nation - Master of the big deal

name: Claus Heinemann
wealthNote: No published personal figure. Gebr. Heinemann is a private family company with €4.3B revenue (2024), owned by two family branches. Claus leads one branch and his cousin Gunnar the other, so a $500M-$1B share is a reasoned estimate.
humbleBeginnings: A fourth-generation heir rather than a self-made founder. The family firm began in 1879, when brothers Heinrich and Carl Heinemann started a tax-free tobacco and liquor wholesale business supplying ships from Hamburg's warehouse district.
breakthrough: Claus and his cousin Gunnar joined in 1979, the company's centenary, and ran it jointly for more than 35 years. They turned a ship and airline supplier, whose first airport retail concession came in 1969, into one of the world's top five travel retailers, operating in over 100 countries (Sydney Airport from 2015).
shieldingStrategy: The firm is still wholly family-owned as Gebr. Heinemann SE & Co. KG. Two family branches share control through a dual leadership kept up for three generations. In 2018 Claus and Gunnar moved to the advisory board and Gunnar's son Max became CEO.

breakthroughDetail.d: The firm began as a tax-free supplier to ships and ferries, then to airlines (Icelandic Airlines, Lufthansa, 1953-54), before opening airport shops (Frankfurt 1958, Cologne/Bonn concession 1969).
It replaced long-time incumbent Nuance as Sydney Airport's duty-free operator (from 2015) and set up regional hubs in Singapore (2009) and Miami (2013).

shieldingDetail.d: Claus, son of Helmut, and Gunnar, son of Horst, come from different family branches. The co-leadership balances the branches instead of handing control to one heir.
The cousins moved to the advisory board in 2018 and installed a fifth-generation CEO with a professional C-suite.
A 2021 arbitration found Heinemann had colluded with James Richardson over the Ben Gurion Airport licence. Tel Aviv courts upheld the ruling in 2022.

sources.label: Tharawat Magazine - The Tale of Gebr. Heinemann
ACROSS - Gebr. Heinemann starts into the fifth generation
DFNI - Gebr Heinemann wins Sydney airport duty-free tender

name: Steven A. Denning
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. Estimate based on four decades as a founding partner, CEO (1995-2006) and chairman of General Atlantic, a firm now managing $100B+. His family's Sage Foundation alone distributed about $12M in 2017.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Salt Lake City and the first in his family to graduate from college. He studied at Georgia Tech and the Naval Postgraduate School, served in the Navy, took a Stanford MBA (1978) and joined McKinsey.
breakthrough: In 1980 he left McKinsey to become the second investment professional at General Atlantic, the captive investment arm Chuck Feeney set up for what became Atlantic Philanthropies. He helped grow it into one of the largest growth-equity firms.
shieldingStrategy: Spent most of his career managing the capital of an anonymous donor. Feeney told the team in 1982 that he had given away almost everything, and General Atlantic invested for the foundation for three decades. His own giving runs through the family Sage Foundation.

breakthroughDetail.d: General Atlantic was founded in 1980 as Atlantic's investment team, led by CEO Edwin Cohen (ex-McKinsey), with Denning as a founding member.

breakthroughDetail.t: From captive fund to outside capital.
breakthroughDetail.d: In the late 1980s the firm began taking money from family offices, foundations and endowments as well as Atlantic. Denning was CEO from 1995 to 2006.

shieldingDetail.d: Steven and Roberta Denning give through the Sage Foundation, which distributed about $12.1M in 2017.
He chaired Stanford's board of trustees and co-chaired the Stanford Challenge. Named gifts include Denning House for Knight-Hennessy Scholars and a $13M gift for the arts (2008).

sources.label: Stanford Magazine - Trustee Who Saw What Was Possible
Inside Philanthropy - Steven and Roberta Denning

name: Shin Kyuk-ho
humbleBeginnings: Born in Korea in 1921, he stowed away to Japan in 1941 to study chemical engineering at Waseda. His first factory was destroyed in wartime air raids, and in 1948 he started Lotte selling chewing gum.
breakthrough: He built Lotte into a Japan-Korea conglomerate, entering South Korea in 1967. Hotel Lotte's duty-free division, founded in 1980, became one of the world's three largest travel retailers alongside DFS and Dufry. In 1988 Forbes ranked him the world's fourth-richest person.
shieldingStrategy: Ran the group through a private Japanese holding company (Lotte Holdings, Tokyo) and an unlisted Hotel Lotte, whose earnings came mostly from duty-free. Fortune called the ownership structure 'convoluted even by the opaque standards' of Korean conglomerates. Opening it up through a 2016 IPO failed amid a prosecution.

breakthroughDetail.d: By 2016 duty-free made up 86% of Hotel Lotte's first-quarter revenue, and Hotel Lotte was the world's third-biggest duty-free operator.
Lotte Duty Free took DFS's Guam airport concession in 2013 (a 10-year, $154M contract). DFS sued, and a Guam court voided the award in 2018, a ruling that was appealed.

shieldingDetail.t: Japanese holding company at the top.
shieldingDetail.d: Lotte Holdings in Tokyo sat above the Korean group, and Hotel Lotte stayed private.
His sons fought for control (2013-15). Younger son Shin Dong-bin won over the elder Shin Dong-joo, whom the founder had favoured.
In 2017, aged 95, he was sentenced to four years for embezzling about $119M from Lotte. He stayed free because of poor health.

sources.label: Fortune - Lotte Group raid casts doubt on IPO (2016)
Pacific Daily/Post Guam - GIAA, DFS appeal to Supreme Court

name: Berry Gordy
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth puts him at $400 million. That fits the documented exits: $61M for Motown in 1988 and $332M for Jobete paid by EMI in three tranches from 1997 to 2004.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Detroit. He boxed professionally until 1950, served in the Army in Korea, and then opened a jazz record store, the 3-D Record Mart, which failed.
breakthrough: In 1959 he borrowed $800 from his family to start Tamla Records, which became the Motown Record Corporation. Motown grew into the leading Black-owned label, and Jobete, its sister publishing company, owned the songs.
shieldingStrategy: He kept the songs (Jobete) in a separate company from the label. He sold the label in 1988 for $61M but held on to Jobete, then sold it to EMI in three stages between 1997 and 2004.

connections.label: longtime friend; Avant later chaired Motown

breakthroughDetail.d: Started Tamla on January 12, 1959 with an $800 family loan, encouraged by Smokey Robinson. The company was incorporated as Motown Record Corporation in 1960.

breakthroughDetail.t: Own the songs, not just the records.
breakthroughDetail.d: Jobete is named after his three eldest children (Joy, Berry, Terry). Its catalog of about 15,000 songs includes 240 he wrote or co-wrote.
Within its first decade Motown had nearly 500 employees and about $20 million a year in revenue.

shieldingDetail.d: He sold Motown Records to MCA and Boston Ventures in June 1988 for $61M and kept Jobete out of the deal.
EMI paid $132M for 50% of Jobete in 1997, then $120M for another 30% in 2003 and $80M for the last 20% in 2004. The later stakes were priced at a preset multiple of revenue.
Selling in tranches let him keep collecting royalties on the unsold share while fixing a price for the rest.

sources.label: Variety — EMI picks up Motown beat (1997)
UPI — EMI buys last of Motown catalog (2004)
Celebrity Net Worth — Gordy's $800 loan to fortune
uDiscover — Gordy tribute to Clarence Avant

name: Jerry Moss
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth reported $700 million at his death in 2023. Over the years, the partners received $500M from PolyGram, a $200M settlement and about $400M in stock for Rondor.
humbleBeginnings: Born in New York City. He studied English at Brooklyn College, served in the Army, and became a record promoter before he and Herb Alpert started a label in Alpert's garage with $200 each.
breakthrough: A&M Records, founded in 1962, grew into one of the largest independent labels. In 1989 he and Alpert sold it to PolyGram for a reported $500 million.
shieldingStrategy: Like Alpert, he held the publishing business (Rondor) apart from the label and sold it on its own to Universal in 2000. He enforced the PolyGram sale terms in court, and he put proceeds into real estate, racehorses and arts philanthropy.

breakthroughDetail.d: Carnival Records (renamed A&M) began in 1962 in an office in Alpert's garage.
PolyGram agreed in 1989 to buy A&M for a reported $500 million. Moss and Alpert stayed on until 1993.
In August 2000 Universal Music Publishing bought Rondor from Alpert and Moss for roughly $400 million. The catalog included the former publishing arms of A&M and Stax.

shieldingDetail.d: The partners sued PolyGram for breach of the sale contract and received an additional $200 million.
Rondor was run and sold apart from A&M, so the songs brought a second exit.
He owned Kentucky Derby winner Giacomo and gave $25M to the LA Music Center in 2020. His heirs listed his Bel Air and Maui estates in 2023.

name: Herb Alpert
wealthNote: Wikipedia cites an estimate of $850 million (2025), and Celebrity Net Worth says $650 million. Both put him in this tier.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, the son of Jewish immigrants from Ukraine and Romania. He started playing trumpet at age eight.
breakthrough: He co-founded A&M Records with Jerry Moss in 1962, launching it with his own hit 'The Lonely Bull'. He was both the label's star act and co-owner.
shieldingStrategy: Same split structure as Moss: label and publishing were sold separately (A&M in 1989 for $500M; Rondor in 2000 for about $400M in stock). Much of the proceeds now go out through the Herb Alpert Foundation.

breakthroughDetail.d: Recorded the label's first hit and kept equal equity with Moss.
$500M from PolyGram (1989), $200M from a breach-of-contract claim against PolyGram, and about $400M in Universal stock for Rondor (2000).
A&M had its headquarters on the old Charlie Chaplin Studios lot at 1416 N. La Brea from 1966 to 1999.

shieldingDetail.d: The Herb Alpert Foundation gave UCLA $30M in 2007 to endow the Herb Alpert School of Music, plus large gifts to CalArts, LA City College ($10.1M) and the Harlem School of the Arts.
The Rondor sale was reported as paid largely in Universal stock.
An even split with Moss avoided control fights over three decades of ownership.

sources.label: Celebrity Net Worth — Herb Alpert's music fortune

name: Ahmet Ertegun
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth puts his net worth at $300 million when he died in 2006. Most of it came from Warner stock received in the 1967 sale, plus art and real estate.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Istanbul, the son of Turkish ambassador Münir Ertegün. He started Atlantic in 1947 with a loan from the family dentist, Dr. Vahdi Sabit, so the start was privileged but not rich.
breakthrough: He co-founded Atlantic Records in 1947 with Herb Abramson and built it into the leading R&B and later rock label. Atlantic also distributed Memphis's Stax Records.
shieldingStrategy: He sold Atlantic to Warner Bros.-Seven Arts in 1967 for $17M in stock but kept running it. That gave him a stake in the parent company (later Warner Communications) while he kept control of the label. He put proceeds into modern art and several homes.

breakthroughDetail.d: Atlantic was financed by family dentist Dr. Vahdi Sabit and held its first sessions in November 1947.
Under the 1965 Stax distribution contract, Atlantic got rights to Stax masters from 1960–67 and kept them when Stax left in 1968.
After Atlantic became part of Kinney/Warner Communications in 1969, he 'wielded considerable influence in the new conglomerate'.

shieldingDetail.d: The 1967 sale was paid in Warner Bros.-Seven Arts stock, tying his fortune to the parent's growth.
Celebrity Net Worth reports he put proceeds into modern art and homes in Southampton, Manhattan, Paris and Turkey.
The Ahmet Ertegun Education Fund pays for university scholarships in the UK, US and Turkey.

name: L.A. Reid
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth reports $300 million. Documented sources include his half of the $100M LaFace buyout (2000), years running major labels, and the 2022 sale of Hitco's catalog to Concord.
humbleBeginnings: Born Antonio Reid in Cincinnati. He started as a drummer in local bands and joined The Deele in 1981, a Solar Records group that also included Babyface.
breakthrough: He and Babyface became a production team for hire and in 1989 formed LaFace Records, an Atlanta label run as a joint venture with Arista. LaFace launched TLC, Toni Braxton, OutKast and Usher.
shieldingStrategy: The label was a 50/50 joint venture: Arista paid for distribution and overhead, and Reid and Babyface owned half the equity. They sold that half to BMG for $100M in 2000. Later he built another partner-owned company (Hitco, with Charles Goldstuck) and sold its catalog to Concord.

breakthroughDetail.d: Reid and Edmonds worked as a production team from 1985, before they had their own label.
LaFace was set up in 1989 as a joint venture with Arista and backed by Clive Davis. It produced 33 number-one singles.
President of Arista (2000–04), then chairman/CEO of Island Def Jam (2004–11) and Epic (2011–17).

shieldingDetail.t: Half the equity, none of the overhead.
shieldingDetail.d: Arista funded and distributed the label; Reid and Babyface owned 50%.
In 2000 BMG (Arista's parent) bought their 50% for $100 million.
Co-founded Hitco Entertainment in 2018 with Charles Goldstuck; Concord bought its recording catalog in 2022 (terms undisclosed).

name: Kenneth "Babyface" Edmonds
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth reports $200 million. Its sources: songwriting and production royalties, LaFace equity (his share of the $100M buyout), and film production.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Indianapolis, the fifth of six brothers. His father died of lung cancer when he was in eighth grade. He played guitar in Manchild and keyboards in The Deele.
breakthrough: As a songwriter-producer for hire he wrote 26 number-one R&B hits. With L.A. Reid he co-founded LaFace Records, where TLC alone sold more than 60 million albums.
shieldingStrategy: He held label equity through the LaFace joint venture until BMG bought it out in 2000. He diversified into film and TV through Edmonds Entertainment Group, co-founded with his then-wife Tracey Edmonds.

breakthroughDetail.d: He wrote and produced 26 number-one R&B hits and won 13 Grammys, mostly for other artists.
LaFace (1989) was a joint venture with Arista; he and Reid owned half.
Edmonds Entertainment produced Soul Food (1997) and Josie and the Pussycats (2001), and executive-produced BET's College Hill.

shieldingDetail.d: BMG bought the founders' 50% of LaFace in 2000 for a reported $100M. That figure was for the whole stake, not his personal payout.
Edmonds Entertainment Group held his film and TV work apart from his music income.
Contemporary reports said his 2007 divorce transferred about $70M in assets.

name: Jimmy Jam
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth reports $40–50 million, based on production fees, songwriting royalties and real estate.
humbleBeginnings: Born James Harris III in Minneapolis. He met Terry Lewis in an Upward Bound program at the University of Minnesota, and both played in Prince's band The Time.
breakthrough: Prince fired them in 1983 after a blizzard stranded them while they were secretly producing the S.O.S. Band for Clarence Avant's Tabu label. 'Just Be Good to Me' became a hit, Flyte Tyme Productions took off, and Janet Jackson's Control followed in 1986.
shieldingStrategy: He works through Flyte Tyme Productions, a private company he co-owns with Lewis that labels hire for production. In 1991 they added label equity through Perspective Records, a joint venture with A&M.

breakthroughDetail.d: Prince dismissed them in 1983. The S.O.S. Band track they had been producing, 'Just Be Good to Me', made their name as producers.
Avant found their production talent at Tabu and later introduced them to Janet Jackson.
Jam & Lewis have 16 Billboard Hot 100 number ones, nine of them for Janet Jackson.

shieldingDetail.d: Flyte Tyme Productions holds their production business. In 2003 it opened a Santa Monica studio, Flyte Tyme West.
Perspective Records (1991) was a joint venture with A&M; its acts included Sounds of Blackness.
He bought a Lake Minnetonka property for $420K in 1987 and sold it for $7M in 2007.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis

name: Terry Lewis
wealthNote: Celebrity Net Worth reports $50 million, mostly production and songwriting royalties.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Omaha, Nebraska. He met Jimmy Jam in Upward Bound at the University of Minnesota and played bass in The Time.
breakthrough: He co-led Flyte Tyme Productions after the 1983 split with Prince. The duo made the S.O.S. Band, Alexander O'Neal and Cherrelle hits for Tabu, then Janet Jackson's Control and more than 100 gold or platinum albums.
shieldingStrategy: He owns his share of Flyte Tyme Productions jointly with Jam. Producer and songwriter royalties pay out over decades, and he added label equity through Perspective Records, the A&M joint venture.

breakthroughDetail.d: Executive Dina Andrews introduced them in 1982 to Clarence Avant; they also worked under producer Leon Sylvers III at SOLAR.
The S.O.S. Band's On the Rise (1983) went gold, followed by Cherrelle's Fragile and Alexander O'Neal's debut.
Control (1986) made them first-call producers for major labels.

shieldingDetail.d: Flyte Tyme Productions holds the partnership's production business.
Perspective Records with A&M (1991) gave them equity alongside fee income.
Writer and producer royalties keep paying long after a record is released, without any further work.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis

name: Kenny Gamble
wealthNote: No reliable published figure exists. The estimate rests on co-ownership of Philadelphia International Records (more than 170 gold and platinum records) and Mighty Three Music publishing, sold to Warner Chappell in 1990.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Philadelphia. As a boy he cut records on arcade recording machines, helped the morning DJs at WDAS, ran a record store and sang with The Romeos, where he met Leon Huff.
breakthrough: With Huff he founded Philadelphia International Records in 1971, with distribution through CBS under Clive Davis. Within two years it was the second-largest Black-owned music company after Motown.
shieldingStrategy: Songs were held in a separate publishing company (Mighty Three Music, with Huff and Thom Bell), and CBS paid for distribution while the founders kept ownership. Later he put money into South Philadelphia property through the nonprofit Universal Companies and his own holdings, including the Royal Theater.

breakthroughDetail.d: PIR signed a distribution deal with CBS Records while the founders kept ownership of the label.
By 1974 Mighty Three Music placed more than 25 Billboard hits a year.
3,500+ songs and 75 RIAA gold or platinum certifications.

shieldingDetail.d: Mighty Three Music, co-owned with Huff and Thom Bell, was sold to Warner Chappell in 1990.

Universal Companies has handled more than $1.5B of development and investment in distressed neighborhoods and runs schools for 5,500+ students. A former CEO, Rahim Islam, was sentenced in 2024 for embezzling from the nonprofit.
PIR was caught up in a 1975 payola case; Gamble was fined.

sources.label: Songwriters Hall of Fame — Gamble & Huff

name: Leon Huff
wealthNote: No reliable published figure exists. The estimate rests on his co-ownership of PIR and of Mighty Three Music (sold to Warner Chappell in 1990), plus writer royalties on more than 3,500 songs.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Camden, New Jersey. He played keyboards in Kenny Gamble's band The Romeos in the early 1960s.
breakthrough: He co-wrote and co-produced the 'Sound of Philadelphia' and co-founded Philadelphia International Records in 1971. Their first big hit together was 'Expressway to Your Heart' (1967).
shieldingStrategy: Same structure as Gamble: the label was co-owned and distributed by CBS, and the publishing sat in Mighty Three Music. He kept a lower profile than Gamble and stayed out of the 1975 payola case.

breakthroughDetail.d: He co-owned both the label and the publisher, not just songwriter shares.
PIR released more than 170 gold and platinum records from 1971 to the early 1980s.

shieldingDetail.d: Warner Chappell bought Mighty Three Music in 1990.
In the 1975 payola case Gamble was fined but Huff was not.
Sony's Legacy Recordings regained PIR's full catalog in 2007 and had fully secured it by 2014.

sources.label: Songwriters Hall of Fame — Gamble & Huff

name: Neil Bogart
wealthNote: No reliable published figure exists. PolyGram paid $15M for half of Casablanca in 1977 and bought the rest in 1980; he used the proceeds to start Boardwalk, then died at 39.
humbleBeginnings: Born Neil Bogatz and raised in Brooklyn's Glenwood Houses. He had a small hit as singer 'Neil Scott' in 1961, then ran Cameo-Parkway's Michigan office.
breakthrough: He ran Buddah Records' operations from 1967, during its bubblegum run, while Buddah also distributed Avant's Sussex label. In 1973 he founded Casablanca, which signed Kiss and became the leading disco label (Donna Summer, Village People).
shieldingStrategy: He started Casablanca with a Warner Bros. loan, paid it back to become independent, then sold half to PolyGram in 1977 while staying in charge. When PolyGram took full control in 1980, he put the proceeds into a new label, Boardwalk.

breakthroughDetail.d: At its peak Buddah and its affiliated labels charted over 100 singles, about one in five releases.
Casablanca nearly went bankrupt in 1975 until Kiss's Alive! hit. It then became the home of disco.
He co-founded Casablanca with Larry Harris, Cecil Holmes and Buck Reingold.

shieldingDetail.d: Warner Bros. financed and distributed the label at first; Bogart asked to be released from the deal and agreed to repay the loan.
He sold 50% to PolyGram for $15M in 1977 and stayed in control. Casablanca then merged with Peter Guber's Filmworks.
PolyGram bought the rest in 1980 and pushed him out over overspending and accounting concerns. After his death, his widow co-founded the Neil Bogart Memorial Fund for pediatric cancer research.

name: Jheryl Busby
wealthNote: No published figure exists. Basis: an undisclosed equity stake in Motown from 1988 that he held when PolyGram bought the label for $301M in 1993, plus years of top executive pay. The low end of this tier is the safe call.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in South Central Los Angeles and left Long Beach State after two years. His first job was inventory clerk at Mattel.
breakthrough: He worked promotion at Stax, A&M and Casablanca, then built MCA's Black music division from scratch (New Edition, Bobby Brown). In 1988 he became Motown's president and CEO after MCA and Boston Ventures bought it from Gordy.
shieldingStrategy: He took equity in Motown rather than just a salary, so he shared in the 1993 sale to PolyGram. He was also a major shareholder in Founders National Bank of Los Angeles, alongside Magic Johnson and Janet Jackson.

connections.label: Avant mentee; chair to his CEO

breakthroughDetail.d: At MCA (1984–88) he built the Black music unit 'largely from scratch'.
He re-signed Diana Ross in 1989 and developed Boyz II Men and Queen Latifah.
When PolyGram bought Motown in 1993 he stayed on as president, with Clarence Avant as chairman.

shieldingDetail.d: He took a stake in Motown when it changed hands in 1988; the size was never disclosed.
Major shareholder in Founders National Bank, described as the first Black-owned national bank.
Head of Black music at DreamWorks (1998–2001), Def Soul Classics (2004) and co-founder of Umbrella Recordings.

name: Al Bell
wealthNote: Low-confidence estimate; no published figure. He owned Stax (one of the largest Black-owned businesses of the 1970s) before it went bankrupt in 1975, and Bellmark's 4x-platinum 'Whoomp!' came before Bellmark's own 1997 bankruptcy.
humbleBeginnings: Born Alvertis Isbell in Brinkley, Arkansas. He worked as a disc jockey in Little Rock before joining Stax in Memphis in 1965 as director of promotions.
breakthrough: In 1969 he became the first African American with equity in Stax, and he bought out Jim Stewart in 1972. He hired Clarence Avant to broker Stax's 1968 sale to Gulf+Western. He also marketed Isaac Hayes's Oscar-winning 'Theme from Shaft'.
shieldingStrategy: Little was protected: Stax's 1972 CBS distribution deal went wrong and Union Planters Bank forced it into bankruptcy in 1975. Bell was tried on bank fraud charges and acquitted. Later he worked through separate small companies (Bellmark, Al Bell Presents).

breakthroughDetail.d: Bell met Avant through NATRA and brought him in to sell Stax to Gulf+Western. The deal closed May 29, 1968 for $4.3M, and Avant took 10% of the debentures.
After Atlantic kept the 1960–67 Stax masters, Bell released 27 albums at once in 1969 to rebuild the catalog, which launched Isaac Hayes as a solo star.
He and Stewart bought Stax back in 1970 with financing from Deutsche Grammophon (the Philips group, later PolyGram).

shieldingDetail.d: Clive Davis left CBS soon after signing the 1972 Stax deal, CBS lost interest, and the label failed.
