Bellmark Records (1989) put out Tag Team's 'Whoomp! (There It Is)' and Prince's 'The Most Beautiful Girl in the World'. It went bankrupt in 1997 and its assets sold for $166K.
Fantasy bought the post-1968 Stax catalog in 1977 for about $4M, and Stax's publishing later became part of Alpert and Moss's Rondor.

sources.label: Arkansas Business Hall of Fame — Al Bell

name: Herb Lotman
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. Estimate rests on his founder stake in Keystone Foods: he sold majority control to Lindsay Goldberg in 2004 and kept a stake through the 2010 sale to Marfrig at $1.26B including debt.
humbleBeginnings: A self-described "West Philly butcher boy" and a butcher's son, he started out in his family's wholesale beef business in Philadelphia.
breakthrough: In the late 1960s he and his partners used cryogenic freezing to mass-produce frozen hamburger patties for McDonald's. Keystone later helped develop the Chicken McNugget and grew past $5B in annual sales.
shieldingStrategy: Kept Keystone private and built almost entirely around one anchor customer. In 2004 he sold majority control to a private-equity firm while keeping a stake, so he took cash off the table before the full exit to Marfrig in 2010.

breakthroughDetail.d: In the late 1960s Lotman and partners pioneered cryogenics for McDonald's and a mass-production system for frozen hamburgers.

breakthroughDetail.t: One customer, almost all the revenue.
breakthroughDetail.d: By 1984 more than 97% of Keystone's business went to the fast-food industry. It supplied McDonald's with beef, chicken and fish.
Keystone ran what trade press called the first total-distribution concept in the McDonald's system. Its logistics arm was later sold to Reyes Holdings' Martin-Brower (2012).

shieldingDetail.d: Sold majority control to Lindsay Goldberg in 2004 but kept a stake until Marfrig bought the company for $1.26B in 2010.
Keystone never listed shares and its products sold under the McDonald's brand, so its founder stayed out of public view.
He left Keystone about six years before his death to focus on philanthropy, including the Macula Vision Research Foundation he co-founded with his wife.

name: J. Christopher Reyes
humbleBeginnings: Eldest of nine children. With his father Joseph and brother Jude he bought a small Schlitz beer distributor in South Carolina for $740,000.
breakthrough: Rolled up more than 130 beer distributors, then bought Martin-Brower, McDonald's main distributor, in 1998 and Great Lakes Coca-Cola Bottling in 2015. Reyes Holdings is now one of the largest private companies in the U.S.
shieldingStrategy: Reyes Holdings stays private and family-owned, with Chris and Jude as co-chairmen and other brothers in executive roles. Distribution is a back-of-house business that consumers never see.

breakthroughDetail.d: Since 1976 the family has acquired more than 130 beer distribution operations, building Reyes Beverage Group.
Bought Martin-Brower in 1998. Its 2012 purchase of Keystone Foods' distribution arm made it McDonald's largest distributor worldwide.
Martin-Brower bought nine distribution centers from Golden State Foods in 2018, and Reyes took one of Perlman-Rocque's four McDonald's centers in 2006.

shieldingDetail.d: Reyes Holdings is privately held and family-owned, so it publishes no shareholder filings.
Chris and Jude co-chair, brother Duke is CEO, and brothers James and Tom run the beverage side.
Sold the Reinhart foodservice unit to Performance Food Group for $2B (2019) and kept the McDonald's and beverage businesses.

sources.label: Reyes Holdings — Origin story: Martin Brower's global expansion

name: Jude Reyes
humbleBeginnings: Born in Washington, D.C., and a Wofford College graduate. He started out with his father and brother running a small South Carolina Schlitz distributor bought in 1976.
breakthrough: Co-built Reyes Holdings from beer distribution into McDonald's main global distributor (Martin-Brower) and a major Coca-Cola bottler. Forbes puts the company's sales at about $51B.
shieldingStrategy: His wealth sits in a private, family-controlled holding company rather than listed stock. He shares control with his brother and keeps a low public profile; Forbes gives him a philanthropy score of 1/10.

breakthroughDetail.t: Bought, not built, the McDonald's lane.
breakthroughDetail.d: Rather than starting a distributor, the brothers bought Martin-Brower (1998) and then Keystone's distribution and logistics businesses from Marfrig (2012).
The Keystone deal added distribution centers in the U.S., Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific.

shieldingDetail.d: Control is split between two co-chairmen, so neither brother's holding has to be marked to market.
Reyes Holdings stays private and family-owned.

sources.label: FleetOwner — Martin-Brower to acquire Keystone Foods operations

name: Mark Wetterau
wealthNote: No published figure. Estimate based on (a) his share of the family's Wetterau Inc., sold to SuperValu for $1.1B in 1992, and (b) Wetterau Associates' position in Golden State Foods: 30% at a ~$400M valuation in 1998, rising to full management ownership in 2004 as sales grew past $5B.
humbleBeginnings: Not a rags-to-riches story. He joined Wetterau Inc., the St. Louis food distributor his great-grandfather founded in 1869, in 1980 and rose to president and COO before the family sold it.
breakthrough: After the 1992 SuperValu sale he co-founded Wetterau Associates with his brother Conrad and Mike Waitukaitis. In 1998 they bought Golden State Foods, one of McDonald's oldest suppliers, together with Ron Burkle's Yucaipa, and he ran it for 25 years as revenue grew from $1.4B to over $7B.
shieldingStrategy: Turned a family business sale into a private family investment vehicle, then bought out the private-equity partner in 2004 to make GSF fully management-owned. In 2024 the family sold control to Lindsay Goldberg but kept a significant stake.

breakthroughDetail.d: Wetterau Inc. sold for $1.1B in 1992. The brothers then formed Wetterau Associates to buy and run food businesses.
In 1998 Yucaipa took 70% of GSF and Wetterau Associates 30%, at an estimated ~$400M deal value.

breakthroughDetail.t: Consolidating McDonald's routes, then selling them.
breakthroughDetail.d: Bought two Perlman-Rocque McDonald's distribution centers in 2006, then sold nine of 27 centers to Martin-Brower in 2018 when McDonald's consolidated its distributors.

shieldingDetail.d: Wetterau Associates LLC held the family's stake, not the brothers individually.
In July 2004 Wetterau Associates bought Yucaipa's 50.3% stake, making GSF "100% management-owned".
Lindsay Goldberg bought a controlling interest in 2024. The Wetterau family kept a significant stake and two board seats.

name: Ted Perlman
wealthNote: No published figure. Estimate based on 40 years of controlling ownership of HAVI, a global McDonald's packaging and logistics group, before a 2014 sale to management, plus a single $25M personal pledge to BBYO in 2019.
humbleBeginnings: A Chicago businessman who started in 1974 with no contract, just a handshake agreement with McDonald's to supply its Chicago-area restaurants. His first deliveries went out four months later.
breakthrough: With partner Bob Rocque he built Perlman-Rocque Distribution and the Perseco packaging business, which made McDonald's red French-fry cartons, into HAVI. HAVI went global from 1981, starting with a Hong Kong office.
shieldingStrategy: Sold HAVI to Staley Continental in 1986 and bought it back in 1988, then kept it private for decades. In 2014 he handed ownership to CEO Russ Smyth and senior managers instead of selling to a strategic buyer.

breakthroughDetail.d: Perlman-Rocque formed in May 1974 on a handshake agreement to serve McDonald's Chicago restaurants.
HAVI is known for McDonald's red fry containers. Perlman said in 2019 that McDonald's was "by far its biggest client".

breakthroughDetail.t: Exit trucks, keep the higher-margin services.
breakthroughDetail.d: In 2006 Perlman-Rocque left McDonald's U.S. distribution and split four centers among Golden State Foods, Keystone Foods and Reyes Holdings.

shieldingDetail.d: Sold to Staley Continental (1986) and bought it back (August 1988), keeping it a private group.
Completed the ownership transfer to CEO Russ Smyth and senior management on Dec 31, 2014. The holding company is now Morgan Street Holdings.
Philanthropy runs through the Harriette and Ted Perlman Family Foundation and multi-year pledges such as $25M over eight years to BBYO.

name: J. R. Simplot
humbleBeginnings: Born in Iowa and raised in Idaho, he left school after eighth grade. He made his first money feeding hogs with a homemade cooker, then moved into potatoes.
breakthrough: Developed commercial frozen French fries. After a handshake agreement with Ray Kroc (dated 1965–67 in different sources), Simplot came to supply more than half of McDonald's fries.
shieldingStrategy: Kept the J.R. Simplot Company private and family-owned. He used its cash to back Micron Technology early, when other investors declined, and diversified into fertilizer, oil and land.

breakthroughDetail.t: Frozen fries solved McDonald's supply gap.
breakthroughDetail.d: Russets were unavailable about three months a year. Frozen product gave year-round consistency, and the switch was complete by 1972.
By the 2000s Simplot supplied more than half of McDonald's French fries.
Provided startup capital to Micron and owned about 20% of it by 1994.

shieldingDetail.d: The J.R. Simplot Company never went public. Forbes listed the fortune as "John Richard Simplot & family."
Fertilizer, oil, ski areas and Micron spread the fortune beyond the fry contract.

shieldingDetail.t: Stayed on the board, not in the spotlight.
shieldingDetail.d: Retired as president in 1973 but stayed involved in the company until his death at 99.

name: Harry J. Sonneborn
wealthNote: He sold his McDonald's stock for about $3 million when he left in 1967, roughly $28M in today's dollars. Claims that he was later worth ~$100M come from a memorial biography and are not corroborated, so the lower tier is used.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Evansville, Indiana, and raised in New York City after both his parents died of tuberculosis when he was five. He was vice president of finance at Tastee-Freez before joining Ray Kroc.
breakthrough: Proposed that McDonald's own or lease the land under its restaurants and sublease it to franchisees through Franchise Realty Corp. Kroc made him McDonald's first president and CEO in 1959.
shieldingStrategy: Put the real estate in a separate company from the franchising business, which gave McDonald's a landlord's cash flow and control over franchisees. Personally, he cashed out his stock in 1967 and lived privately afterward.

breakthroughDetail.d: McDonald's would control the sites and lease them to operators, executed through Franchise Realty Corp.
By 2018 McDonald's real estate holdings were valued at $37.7B, about 99% of company assets per the cited figure.

shieldingDetail.d: Holding sites in a distinct realty entity kept land control and lease income apart from franchise operations.
Resigned in June 1967 after disagreeing with Kroc on expansion, then sold his stock (about $3M).
Moved to Mobile, Alabama, built an estate with a wildlife preserve and collected historical documents.

name: Lorenzo Servitje
humbleBeginnings: Son of Catalan immigrants in Mexico City. He worked in his father's El Molino bakery from age 16 while studying public accounting at UNAM.
breakthrough: In 1945 he co-founded Panificación Bimbo with four partners to make packaged sliced bread. He grew it into the world's largest baking company, which went on to buy Thomas', Entenmann's, Oroweat and, in 2017, McDonald's bun supplier East Balt.
shieldingStrategy: Listed Bimbo in 1980 but kept control in the founding families' hands through private holding companies, led by Normaciel (about 40%), plus other family vehicles and a bank trust.

breakthroughDetail.t: From a family bakery to packaged bread.
breakthroughDetail.d: Ran El Molino before co-founding Bimbo with Jaime Jorba, Jaime Sendra, Alfonso Velasco and José T. Mata.
Bimbo acquired 100+ brands and expanded into the U.S. and Latin America in the 1990s.
In 2017, under his son Daniel, Bimbo paid $650M for East Balt (21 bakeries, 11 countries) to form Bimbo QSR.

shieldingDetail.d: Normaciel is Bimbo's main shareholder. Other blocks sit in vehicles such as Promociones Monser, Philae and Marlupag and in a Banamex trust.
Jorba Servitje, Mariscal Servitje and other relatives sit on the board, and his son Daniel runs the company.
Known for modest habits despite a multibillion fortune.

name: Whitney MacMillan
humbleBeginnings: Not humble. Born in Orono, Minnesota, he was the great-grandson of Cargill founder William Wallace Cargill and the son of Cargill MacMillan Sr.
breakthrough: Led Cargill as CEO from 1976 to 1995, the last family member to hold the job, during a period of rapid growth in turnover. Cargill later became an official McDonald's supplier and bid for Keystone Foods in 2018.
shieldingStrategy: Cargill stayed private, with about two dozen Cargill-MacMillan family members holding roughly 88% and an employee stock plan holding the rest. A mid-1990s family agreement capped family board seats and handed management to professionals.

breakthroughDetail.d: Succeeded Erwin Kelm in 1976 and stepped down in 1995, after which no family member ran the company.
Cargill's annual turnover rose from $10B to $33B over a decade under him.

shieldingDetail.d: Family members held ~88% by 2019 and an ESOP held ~12%.
The family keeps about 80% of net income in the company and pays out roughly 18% as dividends.
A 1990s family agreement limits family directors to six seats (four MacMillan, two Cargill) on a 17-member board.

name: Ronald Burkle
humbleBeginnings: His father managed a Stater Bros. grocery store in Pomona, California, where he stocked shelves and joined the grocery workers' union at 13. He left Cal Poly Pomona without a degree.
breakthrough: Founded Yucaipa in 1986 and ran leveraged buyouts of supermarket chains (Fred Meyer, Ralphs, Food 4 Less) that ended in a $13.5B sale to Kroger. Golden State Foods (1998) was Yucaipa's first deal outside supermarkets.
shieldingStrategy: Invests through private partnerships (Yucaipa, and A-Grade Ventures for tech) rather than a public vehicle, buying, consolidating and exiting businesses instead of holding listed stock.

breakthroughDetail.d: Consolidated Ralphs ($1.5B, 1994), Dominick's and Fred Meyer, then sold the combined chains to Kroger.
Took 70% of Golden State Foods in 1998 (deal valued at ~$400M) with Wetterau Associates as operating partner, and sold out to Wetterau in 2004.

shieldingDetail.d: Yucaipa is a private LLC investing $25–300M per deal, so holdings aren't publicly marked.
Paired Yucaipa capital with operators (Wetterau Associates at GSF) who later bought him out, giving him a defined exit.

name: John Sall
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Rockford, Illinois, studied history at Beloit College and economics at Northern Illinois University, then did graduate work in statistics at NC State, where he met Jim Goodnight.
breakthrough: Co-founded SAS Institute in 1976 and wrote many of its earliest statistical procedures, then created JMP, SAS's desktop statistics product, released in 1989.
shieldingStrategy: Holds about one-third of SAS, which has stayed private and has never taken outside shareholders. He has moved wealth into the Sall Family Foundation and, with his wife Ginger, signed the Giving Pledge in 2012.

breakthroughDetail.t: Joined the NC State project in 1973.
breakthroughDetail.d: Joined the SAS project as a graduate student at NC State and was one of four founders when SAS Institute was incorporated on July 1, 1976.

breakthroughDetail.t: Built JMP as a second product line.
breakthroughDetail.d: Started JMP ('John's Macintosh Project') in the 1980s. Version 1 shipped in October 1989, and he is still its chief architect.

breakthroughDetail.t: Ended up with a third of the company.
breakthroughDetail.d: At incorporation Forbes says Sall and Jane Helwig split 25%. After Barr and Helwig sold out, ownership settled at about two-thirds Goodnight and one-third Sall.

shieldingDetail.d: SAS has no outside shareholders. It considered an IPO in the dot-com era and again from 2021, but has stayed private and debt-free.

shieldingDetail.t: Family foundation and the Giving Pledge.
shieldingDetail.d: Forbes reports nearly $280M contributed to the Sall Family Foundation (conservation, public health, science). The Salls pledged the majority of their wealth in 2012.
The Goodnights and Salls founded Cary Academy (1996) together, and Forbes says the two co-own a country club, hotel and spa in Cary.
