name: Anthony J. Barr
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure. He sold his 40% SAS stake for $340,000 in 1979. The tier rests on four decades of owning the private Barr Systems and a $1M gift he and his wife made in 2021. Low-to-moderate confidence.
peakWealth: Had he kept his 40% of SAS, Forbes (2007) said it would have been worth over $1B
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Summit, New Jersey. Earned physics degrees at NC State (BS 1962, MS 1968) and began writing the Statistical Analysis System there in 1966 for an agricultural research project.
breakthrough: Designed the SAS language, data management and reporting layers, and held the largest stake (40%) when SAS Institute was incorporated in 1976.
shieldingStrategy: Sold out of SAS in 1979 for $340,000, then put his own capital into Barr Systems (founded 1983), a privately held output-management software firm in Gainesville, Florida.

breakthroughDetail.d: Started developing SAS at NC State in 1966 and designed its programming language and systems architecture.
Forbes says he owned 40% of SAS Institute at founding, compared with Goodnight's 35%.
Founded Barr Systems in 1983 to sell HASP remote job entry and output management products for IBM PCs and enterprise printing.

shieldingDetail.d: Sold his SAS shares in 1979 for $340,000 after clashing with Goodnight. It's the clearest counter-example on the map of what holding a private stake can be worth.
Reinvested his career into Barr Systems, his own firm, instead of holding a passive stake.
In 2021 he and his wife Olga gave $1M to Gainesville's Cade Museum, which named a gallery for them.

sources.label: Forbes (2007) — Pampering the customers, pampering the employees (SAS founders' stakes)

name: Judy Faulkner
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Cherry Hill, New Jersey, the daughter of a pharmacist. Studied mathematics at Dickinson College and earned a master's in computer science at the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
breakthrough: Co-founded Human Services Computing (later Epic Systems) in 1979 in a Madison basement with $70,000 from friends and family. Epic grew into the dominant U.S. electronic health record vendor, with $6.7B in 2025 sales.
shieldingStrategy: Never took venture capital, never made an acquisition and never went public. She built a dual-class structure and a perpetual trust that will hold more than 70% of Epic's voting stock after her death, with a voting committee barred from selling or listing the company.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded in 1979 with psychiatrist Dr. John Greist on a $70,000 friends-and-family investment, with no venture capital.
Forbes notes Epic has never made an acquisition and writes all of its own software. Customers include Johns Hopkins and Mayo Clinic.
Forbes puts her ownership at about 42% (Wikipedia: 43% with family).

shieldingDetail.d: Epic has roughly 1 Class A voting share for every 99 non-voting Class B shares, so control and economic value can be separated.

After her death a trust will hold more than 70% of Class A voting stock. A committee of family and long-tenured employees (employees always in the majority) must vote against any IPO or acquisition, and healthcare leaders are named to enforce it.

Signed the Giving Pledge in 2015 for 99% of her wealth. Forbes reports she sells about $100M of non-voting shares back to Epic each year to fund her Roots & Wings Foundation, and the buybacks can feed employee stock plans.

sources.label: Cap Times — Faulkner: I'm leaving it all to charity

name: Dave Duffield
humbleBeginnings: Born in Cleveland and raised in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey. Earned an electrical engineering degree and an MBA at Cornell, then started at IBM in 1964 as a marketing rep and systems engineer.
breakthrough: After three smaller software firms selling to universities and HR departments, he founded PeopleSoft in 1987 with Ken Morris. It became the world's second-largest application software company before Oracle took it over in 2005.
shieldingStrategy: Used Oracle's $10.7B cash takeover proceeds to seed Workday with Aneel Bhusri, keeping control through a dual-class structure, and has moved hundreds of millions into Maddie's Fund and Cornell.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded Information Associates (university exam scheduling), Integral Systems (1972, HR systems for higher education) and Business Software Corp (1979) before PeopleSoft.

breakthroughDetail.t: Fought the hostile bid from inside.
breakthroughDetail.d: On Oct 1, 2004, 16 months into Oracle's hostile bid, PeopleSoft's board fired CEO Craig Conway and made Duffield CEO, with Aneel Bhusri as vice chairman. Oracle closed the deal in January 2005.
Co-founded Workday in March 2005 with Bhusri, funded by his own money plus Greylock, and took it public in 2012.

shieldingDetail.d: Workday's dual-class shares gave Duffield and Bhusri about 67% of voting power after the IPO, which sharply limits takeover risk. Read as a lesson from the PeopleSoft fight.
In 1994 the Duffields endowed Maddie's Fund, an animal-welfare foundation named for their schnauzer, with $200M.
Cumulative Cornell giving now exceeds $550M, including a $371.5M gift in 2026 that renamed the engineering college after him.

sources.label: Cornell Chronicle — Largest gift in university history

name: Joe Liemandt
humbleBeginnings: Dropped out of Stanford in his senior year (1989) to start Trilogy over his father's objections. VCs turned the team down, so they funded it by pyramiding pre-approved credit cards into roughly $500,000 of debt.
breakthrough: Trilogy's sales-configuration software (SalesBuilder) sold to large corporations, and in 1996 he was the youngest self-made member of the Forbes 400 at 27 with $500M. After the dot-com crash he founded ESW Capital (2001) to buy mature software companies for their maintenance cash flow.
shieldingStrategy: Turned down about 20 IPO pitches and kept Trilogy and ESW Capital private. ESW buys software firms and moves work to the Crossover contractor network. He has now pulled about $1B out to fund Alpha School and its AI tutoring platform.

breakthroughDetail.d: Silicon Graphics paid $300,000 for an early configurator demo, three times his asking price.
His father Gregory, formerly head of planning in Jack Welch's GE components division, became Trilogy's chairman and mentored him before dying in 1993.
Forbes says ESW Capital has bought more than 100 small U.S. software companies. Trilogy's buys include Versata (2006) and four Progress Software divisions that became Aurea (2012).

shieldingDetail.d: Kept full private control despite bankers pitching a ~$1B listing in the 1990s.
Acquired businesses sit under privately held Trilogy/ESW Capital, so there are no public filings. Forbes India notes he declines interviews.

Crossover runs about 5,000 contractors in 131 countries on hourly pay with monitoring software, which keeps acquired companies' maintenance revenue largely as cash flow. Critics call it a 'software sweatshop'.

sources.label: Forbes India — Crossover: a software sweatshop

name: Jack Dangermond
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Redlands, California, the son of Dutch immigrants who ran a plant nursery. Studied landscape architecture at Cal Poly Pomona, then urban planning at Minnesota and landscape architecture at Harvard.
breakthrough: His work at Harvard's Laboratory for Computer Graphics and Spatial Analysis led to Esri, which he and his wife Laura founded in 1969 with $1,100 in savings. Its ARC/INFO and ArcGIS software made Esri the leading GIS vendor, with about 40% of the market.
shieldingStrategy: Esri has stayed founder-owned with no outside investors and no debt for more than 55 years. The Dangermonds have signed the Giving Pledge and made the largest gift in The Nature Conservancy's history.

breakthroughDetail.d: Early work at Harvard GSD's Laboratory for Computer Graphics and Spatial Analysis led directly to ARC/INFO.
Esri began as a land-use consultancy and moved into software, releasing Arc/Info (the first commercial GIS) in the 1980s and ArcGIS in 2001.
Revenue reached about $1.1B by 2014, with roughly 4,000 staff by 2016, and was funded from operations.

shieldingDetail.d: Jack and Laura Dangermond control Esri directly. There are no outside investors or external debt, so they answer to no one on valuation or exit.
In 2017 they gave $165M to The Nature Conservancy to protect 24,000 acres at Point Conception, now the Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve.
Esri has pledged $1B of free GIS software to U.S. K-12 schools.

name: Robert F. Smith
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in a middle-class Black neighborhood in Denver, the son of two educators. As a teenager he called Bell Labs every week for five months to win an internship, then studied chemical engineering at Cornell and worked at Goodyear, Air Products and Kraft.
breakthrough: After a Columbia MBA he advised on tech M&A at Goldman Sachs. In 2000 he founded Vista Equity Partners, a private equity firm that invests only in enterprise software and now manages about $100B, with first-fund backing from software billionaire Robert Brockman.
shieldingStrategy: Owns his wealth through a private-equity firm rather than a public company, and has committed it via the Giving Pledge (2017). His early offshore structures did not hold: in 2020 he admitted to concealing income through them and paid $139M under a non-prosecution agreement.

breakthroughDetail.d: At Goldman Sachs (1994–2000) he advised on about $50B of deals involving Apple, Microsoft, eBay, Yahoo and others.
Wikipedia: Robert Brockman 'approached Smith about creating a private equity fund, and offered to back the initial fund'.
Vista has bought enterprise-software firms such as Avalara ($8.4B, 2022) and Nexthink, and Forbes credits it with about 31% annualized returns.

shieldingDetail.d: His fortune sits mainly in his stake in Vista's management company and fund profits. Neither has to be marked publicly the way listed stock does.
Under the October 2020 non-prosecution agreement he admitted to an illegal scheme to conceal income, paid $139M and agreed to cooperate against Brockman.

He was the first African-American man to sign the Giving Pledge (2017). He paid off the Morehouse class of 2019's student debt (~$34M) and gave $50M to Cornell, which named its chemical engineering school for him.

sources.label: NBC News — Robert Brockman dies at 81

name: Brian Sheth
humbleBeginnings: Grew up lower-middle-class in a Boston suburb, the son of an Indian immigrant father and an Irish-Catholic mother, and studied economics at the University of Pennsylvania.
breakthrough: After tech M&A at Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and LBO work at Bain Capital, he joined Robert F. Smith at Vista in 2000. He became president in 2010, was given the co-founder title, and ran deal-making as Vista bought more software companies than any rival.
shieldingStrategy: Built his fortune through his share of a private partnership (Vista) and left the firm in November 2020 after Smith's tax case. He directs his giving through his Sangreal Foundation and Austin-based Global Wildlife Conservation.

breakthroughDetail.d: Worked tech M&A at Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, then on tech leveraged buyouts at Bain Capital.
Joined Vista in 2000 and was president 2010–2020. Forbes credits Vista with more software acquisitions than any competitor in recent years.

shieldingDetail.d: Resigned from Vista in November 2020. Forbes reported the split followed Smith's tax-evasion settlement.
Founded the Sangreal Foundation (2011) for wildlife conservation and chairs Global Wildlife Conservation.

name: Aneel Bhusri
humbleBeginnings: Born in Pittsford, New York. Studied electrical engineering at Brown, worked as a corporate-finance analyst at Morgan Stanley, and earned a Stanford MBA.
breakthrough: Joined PeopleSoft in 1993 and rose to vice chairman under Dave Duffield. After Oracle's takeover he co-founded Workday with Duffield in 2005, while also a Greylock partner, and Greylock backed Workday.
shieldingStrategy: Workday's dual-class shares left him and Duffield with about two-thirds of the votes after the 2012 IPO, so founder control survived a public listing. He and his wife Allison joined the Giving Pledge in 2018.

breakthroughDetail.d: Became PeopleSoft vice chairman and was elected vice chairman again on Oct 1, 2004, the day Duffield retook the CEO job during Oracle's hostile bid.
Greylock partner since 1999 (six-time Midas List). Workday was funded by Duffield and Greylock.
Co-CEO with Carl Eschenbach from 2022, stepped back in 2024, and returned as CEO in February 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: After the IPO Duffield and Bhusri held about 67% of voting shares, which Wikipedia notes greatly reduces hostile-takeover risk.
Joined with his wife Allison in 2018.

name: Robert Brockman
humbleBeginnings: Born in St. Petersburg, Florida, the son of a gas-station owner and a physiotherapist. Graduated from the University of Florida in 1963 and became IBM's top U.S. service-bureau salesman before going out on his own.
breakthrough: Founded Universal Computer Systems in his living room in 1970 to sell car-dealership management software. In 2006 his closely held firm bought Reynolds and Reynolds, a public company nearly twice its size, in a deal valued at $2.8B.
shieldingStrategy: Kept his dealer-software empire private and held other assets through offshore trusts. In 2020 he was indicted on 39 counts for allegedly hiding about $2B in income through them. He died in 2022 before trial, and his estate settled with the IRS in 2025 for $750M.

breakthroughDetail.d: UCS software ran nearly every part of a car dealership's operations, a sticky B2B niche.
The 2006 takeover of Reynolds and Reynolds made the combined private company a 5,000-person operation that Forbes valued at about $5B.
Offered to back Robert F. Smith's first private equity fund, which became Vista Equity Partners.

shieldingDetail.d: Reynolds and Reynolds stayed private under his control after 2006.

shieldingDetail.t: Offshore charitable trust structure tested in court.
shieldingDetail.d: Prosecutors alleged he secretly controlled an offshore trust used to hide ~$2B of gains. He denied it, pleaded not guilty and was found competent in May 2022, but died before trial.
His estate settled with the IRS in December 2025 for $750M, which Wikipedia calls the largest individual tax fraud case.

sources.label: NBC News — Robert Brockman dies at 81

name: J. Pierpont Morgan
wealthNote: Contemporary estimates put his estate at about $68M; biographer Ron Chernow estimated $80M, which Wikipedia equates to about $1.9B in 2024 dollars. The tier uses that inflation-adjusted figure, not a published modern ranking.
humbleBeginnings: Not humble: born in Hartford in 1837 to banker Junius Spencer Morgan, whose father Joseph had co-founded Aetna. He studied at Boston's English High School and the University of Göttingen, then started as a junior clerk at Duncan, Sherman & Co. in New York in 1858.
breakthrough: Built a series of partnerships (Dabney, Morgan; Drexel, Morgan from 1871; J.P. Morgan & Co. from 1895) into America's dominant bank. He reorganized bankrupt railroads, merged Edison's companies into General Electric (1892) and bought Carnegie Steel to form U.S. Steel (1901), the first billion-dollar corporation.
shieldingStrategy: Ran his bank as a private partnership and kept control of reorganized railroads through voting trusts and Morgan partners on their boards. The Pujo Committee (1912) investigated this web of interlocking directorates, and the Supreme Court dissolved his Northern Securities railroad holding company in 1904.

breakthroughDetail.d: In 1879 he quietly sold a large block of William H. Vanderbilt's New York Central stock, much of it in London, without breaking the price. He took a seat on the railroad's board.

He reorganized bankrupt railroads, including the Southern, Erie, Reading and Northern Pacific in 1893–98, installing management and ending rate wars. In 1885 he brokered the truce between the New York Central and the Pennsylvania Railroad.

Drexel, Morgan financed Edison's research. Morgan then merged Edison General Electric and Thomson-Houston into General Electric on April 15, 1892. His Madison Avenue house was the first electrically lit private residence in America (1882).
In March 1901 he bought Carnegie Steel and merged it with Federal Steel and National Steel into U.S. Steel, capitalized at $1.4B. Carnegie personally received about $226M.

shieldingDetail.d: After reorganizing a railroad he kept control through voting trusts, in which shareholders kept ownership but handed their votes to trustees. Morgan representatives stayed on the boards even after the trusts ended.
J.P. Morgan & Co. was a partnership rather than a public company, so its capital and profits stayed among the partners. His son J.P. Morgan Jr. inherited both the firm and its control.
Northern Securities, his 1901 holding company for the Great Northern, Northern Pacific and Burlington railroads, was ordered dissolved by a 5–4 Supreme Court vote on March 14, 1904.

He gave $1,135,000 to Harvard Medical School in 1901, then the largest gift Harvard had received, in honor of his father. His library, opened to the public in 1924, and his art collections went largely to cultural institutions.

sources.label: National Railroad Hall of Fame — J.P. Morgan
Harvard Countway Library — Donors and Fundraising (HMS Quad centennial)
Wikipedia — Northern Securities Co. v. United States

name: Cornelius Vanderbilt
wealthNote: His estate was about $105M in 1877, which Wikipedia equates to roughly $3.17B in 2025 dollars. The tier uses that inflation-adjusted figure.
humbleBeginnings: Born on Staten Island in 1794, he quit school at 11 to work on his father's ferry. At 16 he borrowed $100 from his mother to buy a periauger, a small sailing boat, and ran his own ferry between Staten Island and Manhattan.
breakthrough: Moved into steamboats working for Thomas Gibbons, whose Gibbons v. Ogden victory (1824) broke a state steamboat monopoly. During the Gold Rush he set up the Accessory Transit Company across Nicaragua. From the 1860s he took control of the Harlem, Hudson River and New York Central railroads and merged them in 1869.
shieldingStrategy: Consolidated his railroads into one corporation, the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad, and built Grand Central Depot (1871) to anchor it. He then left about 95% of his estate to his son William Henry so the empire would not be split, a choice the other heirs challenged in a will contest.

breakthroughDetail.d: At 16 he used $100 borrowed from his mother to start a Staten Island–Manhattan ferry, which earned him the nickname 'the Commodore'.

He set up the Accessory Transit Company with others to carry Gold Rush passengers across Nicaragua. After filibuster William Walker seized its Nicaraguan assets in 1855, forces backed by Vanderbilt ousted Walker in 1857.
He took control of the New York & Harlem (1863), the Hudson River Railroad (1864) and the New York Central (1867), and merged the Central with the Hudson River line on November 1, 1869.
His 1868 attempt to corner Erie Railway stock failed after Daniel Drew, Jay Gould and James Fisk issued unauthorized shares.

shieldingDetail.d: He merged his lines into the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad and built Grand Central Depot (1871), so the system ran as a single company.

shieldingDetail.t: Kept the fortune in one pair of hands.
shieldingDetail.d: He left about 95% of his ~$105M estate to William Henry Vanderbilt, and the other heirs contested the will.
In 1873 he gave $1M, then the largest charitable gift in U.S. history, to found what became Vanderbilt University in Nashville.
Wall Street broker Jeremiah G. Hamilton clashed with him over control of the Accessory Transit Company in the 1850s.

name: Andrew Carnegie
wealthNote: His personal share of the 1901 sale to J.P. Morgan was about $225.6M in 5% gold bonds. He gave away about $350M in his lifetime, which Wikipedia equates to $6.9B in 2025 dollars. No single modern net-worth figure is published, so the tier is an inflation-adjusted estimate.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835, he came to Allegheny, Pennsylvania, at 12 in 1848. His first job was as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill for $1.20 a week, followed by work as a telegraph messenger.
breakthrough: Joined the Pennsylvania Railroad under Thomas A. Scott in 1853 and became superintendent of its Western Division in 1859, investing early in sleeping cars, oil and the Keystone Bridge Company. He then built a Bessemer steel empire (Edgar Thomson Works, Homestead) that became Carnegie Steel in 1892 and sold it to J.P. Morgan in 1901.
shieldingStrategy: Kept Carnegie Steel a closely held partnership in which he held a controlling stake. An 'iron clad' partnership agreement let the firm buy out departing partners at book value. After the sale he set out to give the fortune away, as in his 'Gospel of Wealth' (1889), and put the remaining $135M into Carnegie Corporation of New York (1911).

breakthroughDetail.d: He started under Thomas A. Scott at the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1853 and was made superintendent of the Western Division on December 1, 1859.
He put $500 into Adams Express (1855), took shares in Woodruff's sleeping-car company, invested in Columbia Oil (1864) and ran Keystone Bridge, which supplied steel for the Eads Bridge.
He named the Edgar Thomson Steel Works after his old railroad boss, bought Homestead in 1883 and formed Carnegie Steel on July 1, 1892, with Frick, Lauder and Phipps.
He sold to J.P. Morgan in March 1901 and personally received about $226M, mostly in 5% 50-year gold bonds of the new U.S. Steel.

shieldingDetail.d: The agreement let the firm buy out a departing partner at book value. In 1899 Carnegie used it to force out Henry Clay Frick, who sued; Frick settled for shares worth over $30M in the reorganized company.
As controlling shareholder of a private partnership, he could not be removed, and the firm reported to no public shareholders.
Taking gold bonds rather than U.S. Steel shares gave him a fixed income and left him out of the new company's management.

'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' He funded 2,509 libraries (1,679 in the U.S.), Carnegie Technical Schools (1900) and Carnegie Corporation of New York (1911, $135M), and served as a Cornell trustee from 1890 to 1919.

sources.label: Duane Morris — 'Frick v. Carnegie': The Ultimate Minority Shareholder Oppression Suit

name: Elon Musk
peakWealth: $981B (Forbes real-time, Oct 5 2026); Forbes says he became the first trillionaire on June 12, 2026, the day SpaceX listed
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1971 in Pretoria, South Africa. He moved to Canada alone in June 1989, studied at Queen's University and then Penn (physics and economics). In 1995 he was admitted to a Stanford graduate program but never enrolled.
breakthrough: Zip2, which he co-founded with his brother Kimbal in 1995, sold to Compaq in 1999 for $307M, and his 7% stake paid him $22M. X.com merged with Confinity to form PayPal, and eBay bought PayPal for $1.5B in 2002, paying him about $175.8M. He put that money into SpaceX (2002) and led Tesla's 2004 Series A.
shieldingStrategy: He keeps control through founder voting structures. At SpaceX's 2026 IPO his super-voting shares carried over 80% of the votes, and Tesla moved its incorporation from Delaware to Texas in 2024. He signed the Giving Pledge in 2012, and the Musk Foundation held over $14B by the end of 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: Compaq paid $307M in cash for Zip2 in February 1999, and Musk got $22M for his 7%. eBay's $1.5B purchase of PayPal in 2002 paid him about $175.8M for his 11.72%.
He founded SpaceX in 2002 with about $100M of his own money. In February 2004 he put $6.5M of Tesla's $7.5M Series A into the company and became its chairman. In 2008 he also became Tesla's CEO.
In January 2015 Google and Fidelity invested $1B in SpaceX for just under 10%, and Google's Don Harrison joined SpaceX's board. Alphabet disclosed a roughly 6% stake worth $94.1B after the 2026 IPO.

breakthroughDetail.t: Folding xAI and X into SpaceX.
breakthroughDetail.d: xAI (2023) absorbed X Corp in March 2025. SpaceX then bought xAI in an all-stock deal on Feb 2, 2026, valuing SpaceX at $1T and xAI at $250B, and listed on Nasdaq (SPCX) at $135 a share on June 12, 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: Wikipedia says SpaceX's share structure gives Musk over 80% of the votes, which 'effectively prevents anyone but Musk from firing him' as CEO and chair.
After a Delaware court threw out his $56B Tesla pay package, Tesla reincorporated in Texas (June 2024). In November 2025 shareholders approved a new performance award worth up to $1T over 10 years.

He joined the Giving Pledge in April 2012, in the same announced group as John Sall and Sequoia's Michael Moritz. In 2021 he gave about $5.7B of Tesla shares to charity, the same period as his roughly $16B of share sales. The Musk Foundation held over $14B at the end of 2024.
He took Twitter private on Oct 27, 2022 for about $44B, then merged it into xAI and xAI into SpaceX, so the assets moved between companies he controls.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Initial public offering of SpaceX
NBC News — SpaceX gets $1B from Google and Fidelity (2015)
Fox Business — Isaacson on the Musk–Page split

name: Larry Page
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1973 in Lansing, Michigan. His father was a computer science professor at Michigan State and his mother taught programming there. He studied computer engineering at Michigan (1995) and started a PhD at Stanford, where he met Sergey Brin.
breakthrough: His Stanford research project BackRub ranked web pages by the links pointing to them (PageRank). Andy Bechtolsheim wrote a $100,000 check to 'Google, Inc.' in August 1998, before the company existed, and in June 1999 Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia led a $25M round.
shieldingStrategy: Alphabet's Class B shares carry 10 votes each, so Page's 27.4% of the votes and Brin's 25.3% give the two founders majority control (2026 proxy). His wealth is managed by a private family office, Koop. In late 2025, ahead of a proposed California billionaire tax, he reincorporated Koop and other entities in Delaware.

breakthroughDetail.d: He and Brin built BackRub and PageRank as Stanford students, put an early Google on Stanford's site in August 1996, and rented Susan Wojcicki's Menlo Park garage for $1,700 a month.
The June 7, 1999 $25M round was led by Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital. Kleiner's John Doerr still sits on Alphabet's board (2026 proxy).

Google listed on Aug 19, 2004 at $85 a share and raised about $1.67B. Page became CEO again in 2011, made Google part of the Alphabet holding company in 2015, and stepped down as CEO in December 2019.
He and Brin invested in Tesla's $40M third round in May 2006. Google later put money into Musk's SpaceX in 2015.

shieldingDetail.d: Class B shares carry 10 votes, Class A one, and Class C none. As of April 6, 2026, Page held 46.5% of Class B and 27.4% of total votes. Page said the 2004 structure was 'biased toward stability and independence'.
His family office, Koop, manages his investments and properties and has no website. In December 2025 Koop, Flu Lab, Dynatomics and One Aero were reincorporated in Delaware (TechCrunch).
T-Rex LLC, a 2006 entity linked to both founders, became T-Rex Holdings in Delaware on Dec 24, 2025, ahead of a proposed one-time 5% tax on California billionaires.
The Carl Victor Page Memorial Foundation, named for his father, held over $1B in assets as of 2013.

sources.label: TechCrunch — Page loosens business ties to CA (Jan 2026)
Yahoo Finance/BI — Brin and Page moved an LLC out of California
Fox Business — Isaacson on the Musk–Page split

name: Sergey Brin
humbleBeginnings: Born in Moscow in 1973 to a Russian-Jewish family. They emigrated after facing antisemitism and arrived in the U.S. in October 1979. He finished a computer science degree at the University of Maryland at 19 and went to Stanford on an NSF graduate fellowship.
breakthrough: He met Larry Page at Stanford orientation. Together they built PageRank and founded Google in 1998, with venture money from Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia in 1999. Google went public in 2004, and Brin returned to work on Alphabet's AI research in 2023.
shieldingStrategy: His 10-vote Class B shares give him about 25.3% of Alphabet's votes, and together with Page's they form a majority. Since 2005 his wealth has been run by a private family office, Bayshore Global Management, which also has an office in Singapore. In December 2025 he dissolved or moved about 15 California LLCs, several of them to Nevada.

breakthroughDetail.d: His family arrived in the U.S. on Oct 25, 1979. His father became a mathematics professor and his mother a NASA researcher. He finished Maryland in 1993 and earned a Stanford MS in 1995.
He co-developed PageRank with Page, and the company started in Susan Wojcicki's Menlo Park garage. Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia led the $25M 1999 round, and the 2004 IPO raised about $1.67B.
He stepped down as Alphabet president in 2019 and returned in 2023 to contribute to Alphabet's AI research.
He invested in Tesla's 2006 round and backs LTA Research, an airship maker whose Pathfinder 1 got FAA clearance in October 2023.

shieldingDetail.d: As of April 6, 2026 he held 42.9% of Class B shares, or 25.3% of Alphabet's total votes. Class C shares have no vote.

He co-founded Bayshore Global Management with Anne Wojcicki in 2005, after the IPO. It manages about $100B in direct investments and real estate plus the Sergey Brin Family Foundation, and opened a Singapore office in late 2020.

In late December 2025 Brin or his office moved or dissolved at least 15 California LLCs, re-registering seven in Nevada, including vehicles for his yacht and a private air terminal. This came ahead of a proposed one-time 5% California billionaire tax.
Forbes counts over $2B of gifts to Parkinson's research, inspired by his mother's diagnosis. He has not signed the Giving Pledge (not on the pledger list).

sources.label: Yahoo Finance/BI — Brin and Page moved an LLC out of California

name: Sam Altman
humbleBeginnings: Born in Chicago in 1985 and raised in Clayton, Missouri, the son of a dermatologist and a real estate broker. He got his first computer at eight and left Stanford's computer science program after two years in 2005.
breakthrough: Co-founded Loopt in Y Combinator's first 2005 batch and sold it to Green Dot for $43.4M in 2012. He ran Y Combinator from 2014 to 2019, co-chaired OpenAI at its founding in 2015, became its CEO in 2019 and launched ChatGPT in 2022.
shieldingStrategy: Forbes reports he holds no equity in OpenAI. His fortune sits in a personal venture portfolio (Stripe, Reddit, Helion and others) built through Hydrazine Capital, the fund he started with his brother Jack. He and his husband signed the Giving Pledge in 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: Loopt was in Y Combinator's first batch in 2005, raised more than $30M (Sequoia and NEA led the Series A) and sold to Green Dot for $43.4M in March 2012. Altman succeeded Paul Graham as YC president in February 2014.

breakthroughDetail.t: A nonprofit that became a frontier lab.
breakthroughDetail.d: OpenAI launched in December 2015 with Musk and Altman as co-chairs and $1B pledged by backers including Thiel and AWS. Altman became CEO in 2019, and ChatGPT launched in November 2022.
The board removed him on November 17, 2023. Microsoft's Satya Nadella said he would join Microsoft, more than 700 of 770 staff threatened to follow, and he was reinstated on November 21.

breakthroughDetail.t: Won the Musk lawsuit on timing.
breakthroughDetail.d: Musk sued him and OpenAI in February 2024 over the shift away from nonprofit status. On May 18, 2026 an Oakland jury found the claims barred by the statute of limitations; Musk said he would appeal.

shieldingDetail.t: No equity in the company he runs.
shieldingDetail.d: Forbes attributes his entire fortune to outside investments rather than OpenAI stock, so it does not move with OpenAI's valuation.

Hydrazine Capital, co-founded with his brother in 2012, raised a $21M first fund with Thiel as main backer and put most of it into YC companies. Its later funds hold stakes he can diversify across hundreds of companies.
He stepped down as chairman of nuclear startup Oklo in April 2025 to avoid conflicts with OpenAI.
Signed with husband Oliver Mulherin in May 2024, committing most of his wealth to philanthropy.

name: Dario Amodei
humbleBeginnings: Born in San Francisco in 1983 to an Italian-American leather craftsman and a Jewish-American librarian. He studied physics at Caltech and Stanford and earned a Princeton PhD in biophysics in 2011.
breakthrough: After research jobs at Baidu and Google, he joined OpenAI in 2016 and rose to VP of Research, working on GPT-2, GPT-3 and RLHF. He left with six colleagues to found Anthropic in 2021, which private investors valued at $965B in May 2026.
shieldingStrategy: Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation whose Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and elects a growing share of the board. His wealth is a roughly 2% founder stake (Forbes estimate), and he says all seven co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of their wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Princeton biophysics PhD and Stanford Medicine postdoc, then Baidu (2014–15) and Google before joining OpenAI in 2016.

breakthroughDetail.t: Built the scaling playbook at OpenAI.
breakthroughDetail.d: As VP of Research he worked on GPT-2 and GPT-3 and co-invented reinforcement learning from human feedback (Forbes).
Co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six other ex-OpenAI staff, including his sister Daniela as president.

Amazon ($8B) and Google ($3B+) invested from 2023, and Microsoft and Nvidia committed up to $15B in November 2025. The valuation reached $965B in May 2026, and Anthropic filed confidential IPO papers in June 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: As a Delaware PBC, directors may legally weigh the public-benefit purpose against shareholder returns.
An independent trust holds special Class T stock and elects a rising number of directors, reaching a board majority within four years of the Series C.
"All of Anthropic's co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of our wealth" (The Adolescence of Technology, January 2026). Staff pledges are matched by the company.
Forbes estimates each of the seven co-founders owns about 2%, so no single founder holds outright control.

sources.label: Dario Amodei — The Adolescence of Technology (2026)

name: Daniela Amodei
humbleBeginnings: Born in San Francisco in 1987 and went to Lowell High School. She studied English literature at UC Santa Cruz on a classical flute scholarship, then worked in global health and as a communications manager for Rep. Matt Cartwright.
breakthrough: Joined Stripe as an early employee in 2013 and moved to OpenAI in 2018, where she managed teams during GPT-2 and later led safety and policy. In 2021 she co-founded Anthropic with her brother Dario and became its president.
shieldingStrategy: Her wealth is an estimated 2% founder stake in Anthropic, a Delaware public benefit corporation governed partly by its Long-Term Benefit Trust. She is one of the seven co-founders who pledged to donate 80% of their wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Moved from global health and congressional politics to Stripe as an early employee in 2013.
Joined OpenAI in 2018, managed teams during GPT-2's development and then led safety and policy work.

breakthroughDetail.t: Runs the business side of Anthropic.
breakthroughDetail.d: As president since the 2021 founding, she leads the company alongside CEO Dario. Forbes valued each co-founder's stake at $15.5B after the May 2026 round.

shieldingDetail.d: Anthropic's Delaware PBC status and the Long-Term Benefit Trust's Class T stock limit how far ordinary shareholders, founders included, can steer the board.
Covered by the co-founders' pledge to donate 80% of their wealth, announced in January 2026.
She is married to Holden Karnofsky, co-founder of the grantmaker Open Philanthropy.

sources.label: Dario Amodei — The Adolescence of Technology (2026)

name: Alex Karp
humbleBeginnings: Born in New York in 1967 to a Jewish pediatrician and an African-American artist, and raised in Philadelphia. He studied philosophy at Haverford, earned a JD at Stanford Law (where he met Thiel) and a PhD in social theory in Frankfurt.
breakthrough: Started the London money manager Caedmon Group with a $12,000 inheritance, then co-founded Palantir with Thiel and three others in 2003 and became CEO. Palantir direct-listed in 2020 and joined the S&P 500 in 2024.
shieldingStrategy: Palantir's Class F shares, held in a founders' voting trust by Karp, Thiel and Stephen Cohen, carry 49.999999% of the votes regardless of how many shares the founders own. A direct listing let insiders sell without a traditional IPO lock-up.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran Caedmon Group in London for European high-net-worth investors, seeded with a $12,000 inheritance from his grandfather.
Palantir was founded on May 6, 2003. Thiel's fund largely bankrolled the first $30M, and In-Q-Tel put in about $2M.
Listed on the NYSE on September 30, 2020, joined the S&P 500 in September 2024 and moved to Nasdaq in November 2024. Revenue was $4.48B in 2025.
In November 2024 Palantir, Anthropic and AWS agreed to bring Claude to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's AI platform.

shieldingDetail.d: Class F stock keeps the founders' bloc at 49.999999% of voting power as long as they hold a minimum number of Class B shares. Any two of the three founders direct the trust.
Palantir left Palo Alto for Denver in 2020 and announced a move to the Miami area in February 2026.
He lives in Lyman, New Hampshire and is reported to have relocated to Liechtenstein, where he is building a home.

name: Peter Thiel
humbleBeginnings: Born in Frankfurt in 1967, he moved to Cleveland as a baby and spent 1971–77 in South Africa and Namibia before settling in Foster City, California. He studied philosophy at Stanford, co-founded The Stanford Review and earned a Stanford JD in 1992.
breakthrough: Left law and derivatives trading to co-found PayPal in 1998. It merged with Musk's X.com in 2000 and sold to eBay for $1.5B in 2002. He then made the first outside investment in Facebook ($500K in 2004), co-founded Palantir (2003) and Founders Fund (2005).
shieldingStrategy: ProPublica reported, from IRS records, that he grew a Roth IRA from under $2,000 in 1999 to more than $5B by 2019 by buying founder-priced PayPal shares and other early stakes inside it, so the gains can come out tax-free. He also holds founders' voting control at Palantir and gained New Zealand citizenship in 2011.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded with Max Levchin and Luke Nosek in 1998. After the 2000 merger with Musk's X.com it sold to eBay in 2002, and Thiel's 3.7% stake was worth about $55M.
Paid $500,000 for 10.2% in August 2004, joined the board and stayed until February 2022. He has since sold most of the stake.
Incorporated Palantir in May 2003 with Karp and others; his fund largely bankrolled its first $30M. He chairs the company.
Started in 2005 with Ken Howery and Nosek. It was the first institutional investor in SpaceX and Palantir, and it co-led Anthropic's $30B Series G in February 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: Bought 1.7M PayPal founder shares at $0.001 each inside a Roth IRA in 1999. ProPublica reported the account held more than $5B by 2019, tax-free if left until age 59½.
Holds Palantir Class F voting power with Karp and Cohen, which is fixed at 49.999999% of votes.
Invests through Thiel Capital (1996), Founders Fund, Valar Ventures (2010) and Mithril Capital (2012) instead of a single fund.
Granted New Zealand citizenship in 2011, in addition to U.S. and German citizenship.

name: Warren Buffett
humbleBeginnings: Born in Omaha in 1930, the son of a stockbroker who became a U.S. congressman. He was not poor, but he made his own early money from paper routes, pinball machines and selling used cars, bought his first stock at 11, and studied under Benjamin Graham at Columbia.
breakthrough: After working at Graham-Newman he started Buffett Partnership Ltd. in 1956. He did not found Berkshire Hathaway: he bought shares in the failing New Bedford textile mill from 1962, fell out with its manager Seabury Stanton over a tender price, and bought control by 1965. He then turned it into a holding company for insurance float, whole businesses and big stock stakes such as Coca-Cola (1988).
shieldingStrategy: Nearly all his wealth sits in Berkshire stock, which keeps its earnings instead of paying them out, so he has realized little taxable income. He gives the shares away in annual gifts: about $48B to the Gates Foundation from 2006, and since 2026 only to his children's four foundations. The rest is set to pass through a charitable trust run by his three children.

breakthroughDetail.d: He began buying Berkshire Hathaway shares in 1962 expecting a liquidation profit. When Stanton offered less than promised in a tender, Buffett bought control (1965) and fired him. He later called it his biggest investment mistake.
Berkshire used insurance cash to buy whole companies (Geico, Dairy Queen, Duracell) and large stakes. It bought 7% of Coca-Cola for $1.02B in 1988 and still holds about 9%.

In 2008 Berkshire put $5B into Goldman Sachs preferred stock paying 10% (Goldman bought it back for $5.5B in 2011) and $3B into GE preferred. In 2011 it bought $5B of Bank of America preferred with warrants, which it turned into 700M common shares in 2017.
Greg Abel succeeded him as CEO on January 1, 2026. On September 18, 2026 his son Howard Buffett replaced him as chairman, and Warren became chairman emeritus.

shieldingDetail.d: Berkshire keeps its earnings inside the company instead of paying them out, so his fortune grows as unrealized gains on stock he has never sold.
In 2006 he pledged about 10 million Berkshire B shares to the Gates Foundation over his lifetime. The foundation received about $48B in all. He served as a trustee until June 2021.

His July 2026 gift of about $6B in Berkshire shares left out the Gates Foundation for the first time in 20 years. It went to the Susan Thompson Buffett, Howard G. Buffett, Sherwood and NoVo foundations instead.
He launched the Giving Pledge with Bill Gates in 2010 and has committed more than 99% of his wealth to philanthropy.

sources.label: Fortune — Buffett ends Gates Foundation donations (Jul 2026)

name: Stephen A. Schwarzman
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in the Philadelphia suburbs, where his father owned a dry-goods store. At 14 he started a lawn-mowing business, finding the clients while his younger twin brothers did the mowing. He went on to Yale and Harvard Business School.
breakthrough: He ran mergers and acquisitions at Lehman Brothers, then left in 1985 to co-found Blackstone with his former Lehman boss Peter Peterson, with $400,000 of their own money. Blackstone grew from an M&A boutique into the world's largest alternative-asset manager, with about $1.3 trillion under management by 2026.
shieldingStrategy: His fortune is his Blackstone stake and his share of the fees and carried interest it earns. He took the firm public in 2007 but stayed chairman and CEO. He has tied his name to large institutional gifts and signed the Giving Pledge in 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: Peterson and Schwarzman, both from Lehman, founded Blackstone in 1985 with $400,000 of seed capital. The name joins 'Schwarz' (black) and 'Peter' (stone).

In 1987 Blackstone backed Larry Fink's bond team in a 50-50 venture that became BlackRock. Blackstone sold its stake to PNC for $240M in the mid-1990s, which Schwarzman later called his worst business decision.
Blackstone bought Hilton Hotels for about $26B including debt in 2007, took it public again in 2013 and was fully out by 2018, with roughly $14B of profit.
Blackstone joined KKR, Goldman Sachs and others in the $11.3B SunGard buyout (2005).

shieldingDetail.d: The June 2007 IPO sold a 12.3% stake for $4.13B. Schwarzman stayed chairman and CEO, with Jonathan Gray as president.
In 2025 his total compensation from Blackstone was about $1.24B.
His gifts include $100M to the New York Public Library, $100M for Schwarzman Scholars at Tsinghua, $350M to MIT for a computing college, $150M to Yale and £150M to Oxford.
He signed the Giving Pledge in 2020.

name: Henry Kravis
humbleBeginnings: Not humble: born in Tulsa in 1944, the son of Raymond Kravis, a successful oil engineer who had been a business partner of Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. He went to Loomis Chaffee, Claremont McKenna and Columbia Business School.
breakthrough: At Bear Stearns he, his cousin George Roberts and their boss Jerome Kohlberg did early 'bootstrap' buyouts of family companies. They left in 1976 to found Kohlberg Kravis Roberts. The firm's debt-financed buyouts of Beatrice (1986) and RJR Nabisco (1989, about $25B, financed with Drexel junk bonds) defined the 1980s LBO era.
shieldingStrategy: He has held control through KKR's partnership structure. Even after KKR listed (2010) and became a corporation, KKR Management LLP, owned by him and Roberts, kept control. A 2021 reorganization ends that control on the 'Sunset Date' (no later than December 31, 2026). His wealth also funds named gifts to Columbia, Memorial Sloan Kettering and Loomis Chaffee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Kohlberg, Kravis and Roberts did leveraged deals at Bear Stearns, including Orkin Exterminating (1964), before going independent in 1976.

KKR bought Beatrice in 1986 and sold it off in pieces. Its international food arm went to Reginald Lewis for $985M in 1987. Black Enterprise reports that Kravis doubted Lewis's credibility until Michael Milken vouched for him.

KKR won RJR Nabisco at $109 a share against a management bid backed by Shearson Lehman Hutton. At about $25B ($31B including debt) it was the largest LBO in history. Drexel Burnham Lambert raised about $5B of the financing as junk bonds.
KKR led the $44B TXU buyout (2007) with TPG and Goldman Sachs, and joined Blackstone and others in the 2005 SunGard deal.

shieldingDetail.d: Under the October 2021 Reorganization Agreement, KKR Management LLP's control through Series I Preferred Stock ends on the Sunset Date, after which voting becomes one vote per share.
In 2021 he and Roberts handed the co-CEO roles to Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall but stayed on as executive co-chairmen.

He has given $100M to Columbia Business School (2010) plus $25M (2015), $100M to Memorial Sloan Kettering (2022) and $100M to Loomis Chaffee (2024). His wife Marie-Josée Kravis chairs the board of MoMA.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Inside Reginald Lewis' Beatrice acquisition

name: George R. Roberts
humbleBeginnings: Born in Houston in 1943 into a well-off family. He went to Culver Military Academy, Claremont McKenna College (1966) and UC Hastings law school, then joined his cousin Henry Kravis at Bear Stearns, where he made partner at 29.
breakthrough: He co-founded KKR in 1976 with Kravis and Jerome Kohlberg. By 1978 KKR had raised its first institutional fund. Together they made the leveraged buyout an institutional asset class, from Beatrice and Safeway (1986) to RJR Nabisco.
shieldingStrategy: He shares the founders' control of KKR through KKR Management LLP, which ends on the 2021 agreement's Sunset Date (no later than December 31, 2026). He is executive co-chairman. His giving goes mainly through REDF, the employment social-enterprise fund he founded, and to Claremont McKenna.

breakthroughDetail.d: At Bear Stearns the future KKR partners did early leveraged acquisitions such as Orkin Exterminating (1964).
By 1978 KKR had raised its first institutional fund with outside investor commitments.
KKR's $5.5B Safeway buyout (1986) was a friendly deal that helped management fend off hostile bidders.
He co-led the 1988–89 RJR Nabisco buyout, the largest LBO of its era, which became the subject of 'Barbarians at the Gate.'

shieldingDetail.d: Under the October 2021 Reorganization Agreement, KKR Management LLP's Series I control ends on the earlier of December 31, 2026, or six months after both founders have died or become disabled.
He founded REDF (Roberts Enterprise Development Fund), which funds businesses that employ people facing barriers to work.
He gave Claremont McKenna $50M in 2012 and $140M in 2022.

name: Marc Rowan
humbleBeginnings: Born on Long Island in 1962 and raised in Hollywood, Florida. His father worked in auto leasing and his mother was a teacher. After his father died, the University of Pennsylvania let him finish at Wharton despite the family's financial hardship. He earned a BS and an MBA there.
breakthrough: He joined Drexel Burnham Lambert's M&A group in 1985. When Drexel collapsed in 1990, he co-founded Apollo with fellow Drexel bankers Leon Black and Josh Harris. Apollo bought the distressed debt of failed insurers and S&Ls and converted it into control. Rowan built its insurance engine, Athene, after 2008, became CEO in 2021, and saw Apollo pass $1 trillion in assets in 2026.
shieldingStrategy: His wealth is his Apollo stake. The three founders together kept about 58% of Apollo after its 2011 IPO. Separately, he owns Hamptons and North Fork restaurants through Montauk Asset Holdings. His philanthropy runs through Penn (a $50M Wharton gift in 2018) and UJA-Federation of New York, which he chairs.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rowan, Black and Harris met in Drexel's M&A department and founded Apollo in 1990, after the junk-bond house went bankrupt.
Apollo's first big trade, alongside Credit Lyonnais, was buying the junk-bond portfolio of the seized Executive Life Insurance Company.
Apollo and TPG bought Harrah's Entertainment in 2008 for about $27.8B including debt. Rowan joined the board when the deal closed, and Harrah's was later renamed Caesars.
He helped found the annuity company Athene after 2008. Apollo bought it outright in an $11B all-stock deal in January 2022, one of his first major deals as CEO.

shieldingDetail.d: Apollo listed on the NYSE in 2011, with the three co-founders holding 58%, and joined the S&P 500 in December 2024.
He owns Hamptons-area restaurants, including Duryea's Lobster Deck, through Montauk Asset Holdings.
His $50M gift to Wharton (2018) was the school's largest at the time, and he chaired Wharton's board of advisors until 2025.

name: Charles Schwab
humbleBeginnings: Born in Sacramento in 1937, the son of a lawyer who served as a district attorney. He grew up in Woodland and Santa Barbara, sold ice cream and caddied as a boy, and got through Stanford while struggling with dyslexia, which wasn't diagnosed until he was about 40.
breakthrough: He started First Commander Corp. in San Francisco in 1971, with $100,000 borrowed from an uncle, and renamed it Charles Schwab & Co. in 1973. After the SEC deregulated commissions in 1975, he cut his prices roughly in half and paid brokers salaries instead of commissions. That turned Schwab into the leading discount broker, which later bought TD Ameritrade (2020).
shieldingStrategy: He sold the company to Bank of America in 1983 for $55M and bought it back in 1987, so he kept founder control and the later gains. He still owns about 6% of the public company and is chairman. He moved his residence to Florida after selling his San Francisco home in 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: When the SEC ended fixed brokerage commissions, Schwab halved his prices, paid salaries instead of commissions and added toll-free, round-the-clock phone trading.
Bank of America bought Schwab in 1983 for $55M. Management, led by Schwab, bought it back in 1987, and he took it public that year.
Schwab bought U.S. Trust for $2.73B (2000) and sold it to Bank of America for $3.3B (2007), then bought TD Ameritrade in 2020.

shieldingDetail.d: He still holds about 6% of the Charles Schwab Corporation and stayed chairman after stepping down as CEO in 2008.
Repurchasing the firm from Bank of America before the 1987 IPO put the later growth in his hands rather than the bank's.
After learning of his own dyslexia through his son's diagnosis, he became a backer of research and support for children with learning differences.

name: Thomas Peterffy
humbleBeginnings: Born in Budapest in 1944, during a Soviet air raid. He reached New York in 1965 with almost nothing and worked as an architectural draftsman, then as a computer programmer, including at the commodities trader Mocatta Metals.
breakthrough: In 1977 he bought an American Stock Exchange seat for about $36,000 and traded options as a market maker using his own pricing models. His firm Timber Hill brought handheld computers onto the trading floor in the early 1980s. In 1993 he spun its technology out as Interactive Brokers, a low-cost electronic broker that went public in 2007.
shieldingStrategy: He controls Interactive Brokers through IBG Holdings LLC, which held about 73.5% of the operating company in 2026, while the listed shares hold the rest. The 2007 IPO floated only 10%. He also owns more than 560,000 acres of land, mostly in Florida.

breakthroughDetail.d: He saved about $200,000 as an engineer-programmer and in 1977 bought an AMEX seat for $36,000 to trade options.
T.P. & Co. became Timber Hill in 1982 and introduced handheld computers to trading floors in the early 1980s.
Interactive Brokers was incorporated in 1993 to offer Timber Hill's execution technology to customers. It went public on Nasdaq in May 2007 by selling 10% in a Dutch auction.
In 2020 Interactive Brokers took over Folio Investments' retail business from Goldman Sachs.

shieldingDetail.d: IBG Holdings LLC held 73.5% of IBG LLC's membership interests and about 73.7% of the voting power in 2026, while public shareholders held 26.5%.
Forbes counts him among the largest landowners in the U.S., with more than 560,000 acres, mostly in Florida.
He handed the CEO role to Milan Galik in 2019 and remains chairman and the controlling shareholder.

name: Carl Icahn
humbleBeginnings: Born in Brooklyn in 1936 and raised in Far Rockaway, Queens. His father was a cantor and substitute teacher and his mother a schoolteacher. He studied philosophy at Princeton (1957), briefly attended NYU medical school, and served in the Army Reserve before becoming a stockbroker at Dreyfus in 1961.
breakthrough: In 1968 he bought a New York Stock Exchange seat with $150,000 of his own money and $400,000 from an uncle. From Tappan (1978) onward he bought stakes in undervalued companies and forced sales or buybacks. Drexel's 'highly confident' letter, first written for his Phillips Petroleum raid, gave him a way to finance threatened takeovers. TWA (1985), Texaco, USX and RJR Nabisco followed, and later Netflix, Apple, Dell and eBay.
shieldingStrategy: He holds about 86% of Icahn Enterprises, a publicly traded master limited partnership that holds his businesses, and stopped managing outside money in 2011. A 2023 Hindenburg short report showed he had pledged much of his stake for personal loans, and in 2024 he paid a $500,000 SEC penalty over that disclosure without admitting wrongdoing.

breakthroughDetail.d: Drexel first used the letter in Icahn's attempt on Phillips Petroleum. Leon Black, later an Apollo founder, was the lead banker. Icahn didn't win control but sold his shares back at a profit.

He took 50% of Trans World Airlines in 1985 and bought the rest in a 1988 LBO, then sold assets such as its London routes ($445M to American, 1991). Wikipedia says he made $469M and left TWA with $540M of debt.

He announced a bid for USX (U.S. Steel) on October 6, 1986, and dropped it in early 1987. From 1995 to 2000, at first alongside Bennett LeBow, he ran four proxy fights to force RJR Nabisco to split off its food business.
He took a 10% Netflix stake in 2012, campaigned for Apple buybacks in 2013–14, sued to derail Michael Dell's $24.4B buyout in 2013, and pushed eBay to spin off PayPal in 2014.

shieldingDetail.d: Icahn Enterprises (formerly American Real Estate Partners) is a Nasdaq-listed limited partnership, about 86% owned by him, that holds energy, auto, food-packaging and real-estate businesses.

In 2024 the SEC fined Icahn Enterprises $1.5M and Icahn $500,000 for not disclosing that his units were pledged for personal loans. Neither admitted wrongdoing. The partnership halved its distribution in August 2023.
He signed the Giving Pledge in 2010 and has given about $200M to Mount Sinai, whose medical school now bears his name.

name: Phil Knight
peakWealth: $24.4B (Forbes real-time, Oct 5 2026); Wikipedia cites $35.4B as of October 2025
humbleBeginnings: Born in Portland, Oregon in 1938, he ran track at the University of Oregon under coach Bill Bowerman (B.B.A. 1959). At Stanford's business school (MBA 1962) he wrote a paper asking whether Japanese running shoes could do to German shoes what Japanese cameras had done to German cameras. After graduating he sold Japanese running shoes from the trunk of his car.
breakthrough: In 1962 he found Onitsuka Tiger shoes in Kobe and became their U.S. distributor. On Jan 25, 1964 he and Bowerman each put in $500 to start Blue Ribbon Sports, which became Nike in 1971. Nike went public in December 1980, by which time it had about half the U.S. athletic-shoe market, and FY2025 revenue was $46.3B.
shieldingStrategy: Control runs through Nike's two share classes: Class A elects three-quarters of the board. Knight moved his Class A shares into Swoosh, LLC in 2015 and sold its voting units to a trust of his son Travis in 2016. He gives through the Knight Foundation and large gifts to Stanford, Oregon and OHSU.

breakthroughDetail.d: Blue Ribbon Sports started in Eugene as a distributor for Onitsuka Tiger, funded with $500 each from Knight and Bowerman on a handshake, then launched its own Nike brand in 1971.
He commissioned the Swoosh from designer Carolyn Davidson for $35 in 1971 and later gave her a few hundred shares when the company went public.
Nike listed in December 1980 with about 50% of the U.S. athletic-shoe market. It bought Converse for $309M in 2003 and was #90 on the 2025 Fortune 500.

shieldingDetail.t: Class A shares elect most of the board.
shieldingDetail.d: Nike's Class A holders elect three-fourths of the directors, so the founder's block keeps control even though most traded stock is Class B.

Knight put his Class A stock (257M shares after the 2015 split) into Swoosh, LLC. On June 30, 2016 he sold its voting units to an entity of the Travis A. Knight 2009 Irrevocable Trust II and left Nike's board, so control passed to his son without breaking up the block.

Forbes counts $4.5B given, mainly through the Knight Foundation, including $105M (2006) to Stanford GSB, $400M (2016) for Knight-Hennessy Scholars, over $2B to Oregon and a $2B pledge (2025) to OHSU's Knight Cancer Institute.

name: Ralph Lauren
humbleBeginnings: Born Ralph Lifshitz in the Bronx in 1939 to Jewish immigrant parents, he worked as a teenage stock boy and changed his surname to Lauren at 16. After Army service he sold at Brooks Brothers and then sold ties for Beau Brummell.
breakthrough: In 1967, at 28, he talked Beau Brummell's president into letting him launch his own line of ties, working from a single drawer in the Empire State Building. Neiman Marcus ordered 1,200 ties, the Polo menswear line followed in 1968 and women's wear in 1971. The company listed on the NYSE on June 12, 1997.
shieldingStrategy: He kept voting control through high-vote Class B stock, which Forbes puts at 85% of the votes. He sold 28% of the company to a Goldman Sachs fund in 1994 for $135M and floated it in 1997, taking cash out while keeping control. He stepped down as CEO in 2015 but stayed executive chairman and chief creative officer.

breakthroughDetail.d: He started with men's ties in 1967; a 1,200-tie order from Neiman Marcus put the brand into department stores.
Menswear under the Polo name (1968), women's wear (1971), the costumes for The Great Gatsby (1974), fragrances (1978) and the Rhinelander mansion flagship (1986) widened it into a lifestyle label.
Licensees such as Reed & Barton and WestPoint Stevens made Home Collection products under the brand, extending it without the company building every factory.

shieldingDetail.d: In 1994 he sold 28% to a Goldman Sachs investment fund for $135M. His stake was worth over $400M after the 1997 listing.
Forbes reports he controls 85% of the voting rights, so outside holders cannot replace him.
His son David is chief branding and innovation officer, and Lauren remains executive chairman and chief creative officer after giving up the CEO role in 2015.
He owns the 17,000-acre Double RL ranch in Colorado (bought from 1982) and a car collection valued at over $600M.

name: Brian Chesky
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1981 in Niskayuna, New York, the son of two social workers. He studied industrial design at the Rhode Island School of Design (BFA 2004) and was earning about $40,000 a year as a designer when he moved to San Francisco in 2007.
breakthrough: In October 2007 he and RISD classmate Joe Gebbia rented air mattresses in their apartment during a design conference; Nathan Blecharczyk joined as technical co-founder. They kept going by selling 'Obama O's' and 'Cap'n McCain's' cereal boxes, got $20,000 from Y Combinator in early 2009 and $600,000 from Sequoia that April. Airbnb listed on Nasdaq on Dec 10, 2020, raising $3.5B.
shieldingStrategy: Airbnb's dual-class shares give him about 11% of the economics and roughly a third of the votes. He signed the Giving Pledge in 2016 and in 2022 pledged $100M with the Obamas for the Voyager Scholarship.

breakthroughDetail.d: Election-themed cereal boxes raised about $20,000–$30,000 to pay the founders' debts before outside money arrived.

Y Combinator's Winter 2009 batch gave $20,000 for 6%. Sequoia put in $600,000 of seed in April 2009, and joined Greylock in the $7.2M Series A (November 2010). Founders Fund led a $200M round in 2012.
In April 2020 Silver Lake and Sixth Street provided $1B of equity and $1B of debt at 9%–11.5%. Eight months later the IPO raised $3.5B, and Sequoia's $375M of investments were worth about $15B.

shieldingDetail.d: Wikipedia gives his stake as 10.7% economic and 31.9% voting, so the three founders together keep effective control.
He joined the Giving Pledge in 2016, and in 2022 pledged $100M to the Obama Foundation's Voyager Scholarship.
Sam Altman credited Chesky and Ron Conway with steadying him during his November 2023 removal from OpenAI; Chesky publicly backed him and advised him through his return.

sources.label: Fortune — Sequoia's Alfred Lin on Airbnb and DoorDash
TechCrunch — Airbnb confirms $200M round led by Founders Fund
Skift — Chesky's role in Altman's return

name: Tony Xu
humbleBeginnings: Born in Nanjing, China around 1984, he came to the U.S. as a small child and grew up in Champaign, Illinois. His mother, a doctor in China, worked as a server in a Chinese restaurant before opening acupuncture clinics. He studied industrial engineering at UC Berkeley and worked at PayPal, eBay, McKinsey and Square before Stanford's business school (MBA 2013).
breakthrough: With Stanford classmates Andy Fang, Stanley Tang and Evan Moore he ran PaloAltoDelivery.com (2012), which became DoorDash in January 2013. Y Combinator gave $120,000 for 7% that summer, and Sequoia led a $17.3M Series A in 2014. The December 9, 2020 IPO raised $3.37B, and DoorDash later bought Wolt (€7B, 2021) and Deliveroo ($3.9B, 2025).
shieldingStrategy: He owns about 4.6% of DoorDash but held voting authority over all Class B shares, about 69% of the votes at the IPO. He and his wife Patti signed the Giving Pledge.

breakthroughDetail.d: PaloAltoDelivery.com (2012) tested whether local restaurants wanted delivery; it became DoorDash in January 2013.
Sequoia's Alfred Lin initially passed, then led the $17.3M Series A in May 2014 and joined the board. Sequoia invested $415M in total, worth over $8.5B after the IPO.
DoorDash bought Caviar from Square for $410M (2019), Wolt for €7B (2021) and Deliveroo for $3.9B (2025).

shieldingDetail.d: Wikipedia says he held voting authority over all Class B shares, 69% of the votes as of December 2020, while owning about 5% economically.
