He led a roughly $22B management buyout in 2006-07 with Goldman Sachs and others, then took Kinder Morgan back to the NYSE in February 2011 in what was then the largest private-equity-backed IPO in US history.
In 2014 he folded KMP, KMR and El Paso Pipeline Partners into one public company, Kinder Morgan Inc.

shieldingDetail.d: Company proxies record that from October 1999 he took an annual salary of $1 'to demonstrate his belief in the company's long term viability'.
He rolled his stake into the 2007 take-private and kept a large share of the company it became, so his wealth is mostly KMI stock rather than pay.
He and his wife Nancy started the Kinder Foundation in 1997. It has committed more than $850M, mostly in Houston. They are also Giving Pledge signers.

name: Harold Hamm
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1945 in Lexington, Oklahoma, the 13th and youngest child of cotton sharecroppers. He started working at a gas station at 16 and then took oil-refinery work. Before drilling, he ran a trucking business hauling water for oilfields.
breakthrough: Founded Shelly Dean Oil in 1967, named for his two daughters, and renamed it Continental Resources in 1990. Continental found the Cedar Hills field in North Dakota in 1995. In 2004 it completed the first commercially successful horizontal, fracked well in the North Dakota Bakken, a key step in the US shale boom.
shieldingStrategy: Took Continental public in 2007, then in November 2022 his family bought out the public shareholders for $4.3B in cash. The company is now 100% owned by the Harold Hamm Family LLC. He is a Giving Pledge signer.

breakthroughDetail.d: Started with a single company in 1967, borrowed to drill his own wells, and grew without an outside sponsor.
Discovered North Dakota's Cedar Hills field, described as the 7th-largest onshore field in the lower 48 states by liquid proved reserves.
In 2004 Continental drilled the first commercially successful horizontally drilled and fracked well in the North Dakota Bakken.
At the 2007 IPO Hamm sold about $300M of shares and kept control.

shieldingDetail.d: In November 2022, Hamm family affiliates acquired the shares they did not already own for about $4.3B, so Continental no longer reports to public shareholders.
Continental is now held 100% by the Harold Hamm Family LLC, and Forbes notes that ownership was distributed among family members in the buyout.
His 2014 divorce from Sue Ann Arnall ended with a payment of about $975M, one of the largest settlements on record.
He has signed the Giving Pledge and funded the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma.

name: Leonard Schleifer
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1953 in Queens, the son of a sweater manufacturer who had been a WWII codebreaker. He went to Cornell on scholarship, then earned an MD-PhD at the University of Virginia under future Nobel laureate Alfred Gilman. He was teaching at Weill Cornell when he started the company.
breakthrough: Co-founded Regeneron in 1988 with scientist George Yancopoulos, starting with $1 million of seed money from Merrill Lynch venture capitalist George Sing. He took it public in 1991. Eylea (approved 2011) and Dupixent (2017) became blockbusters, and Regeneron now has 12 FDA-approved medicines.
shieldingStrategy: Has run Regeneron since founding and controls it through its pre-IPO Class A stock, which carries ten votes per share. His wealth is his stake of about 2% of the common stock. Partnerships, mainly with Sanofi and later BARDA, paid for much of the research so the founders were not heavily diluted.

breakthroughDetail.d: Schleifer, a neurologist teaching at Cornell, recruited Yancopoulos, and the two have run the company together since 1988.
Eylea (aflibercept), approved in November 2011 for age-related macular degeneration, made Schleifer a billionaire. It brought in $4.8B in US sales in 2024.
Sanofi took a stake in 2007 and funded collaborative development. In 2020 Regeneron bought back about 19.2M of Sanofi's shares for around $5B.
Under a 2017 BARDA agreement the US government funded 80% of development for some antibody drugs, and that platform later produced the REGEN-COV COVID-19 antibodies.

shieldingDetail.d: Regeneron's 2025 proxy says Class A stock carries ten votes per share and none has been issued since the 1991 IPO. Schleifer holds most of the roughly 1.8M Class A shares outstanding.
His 2014 compensation of about $42M, the highest among biopharma CEOs that year, came mostly in stock awards, which built his ownership.
Using Sanofi and BARDA money for R&D meant fewer new shares had to be sold, preserving the founders' stakes.

name: Alan B. Miller
wealthNote: Forbes does not list him. The 2025 UHS proxy shows him beneficially owning about 8.0M shares across Classes A, B and C (5.16M Class A, 0.66M Class C, and Class B including conversions), worth about $1.4B at $175.72 (Oct 2, 2026). Part of this is held in LLCs and 2024 GRATs for his children, so his personal share may be lower. Tiered conservatively at $500M-$1B because part of the ~8.0M beneficially owned UHS shares sits in his children's trusts and LLCs.
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1937 in Brooklyn to immigrant parents. His father owned a dry-cleaning store and his mother worked for a millinery company. He studied at William & Mary and earned a Wharton MBA.
breakthrough: In 1973 he took over struggling hospital chain American Medicorp and turned it around, but lost it to a hostile takeover by Humana in 1978. In April 1979 he founded Universal Health Services with six employees and no revenue. UHS owned four hospitals within 18 months, went public in 1981, and became a Fortune 500 hospital and behavioral-health operator, helped by the $3.1B Psychiatric Solutions deal in 2010.
shieldingStrategy: Built a multi-class share structure: he holds all of the Class C stock (100 votes per share) and about 78% of Class A, which gives him about 88% of UHS's voting power while owning a small part of its equity. In 2021 he handed the CEO role to his son Marc and became executive chairman.

breakthroughDetail.d: His American Medicorp turnaround earned industry recognition but ended when Humana won a hostile bid in 1978, which pushed him to start a company he could control.
Within 18 months of its 1979 founding UHS owned four hospitals and managed two more. It listed in 1981 and joined the S&P 500 in 2014.
The $3.1B purchase of Psychiatric Solutions (2010), followed by Cygnet in the UK and other deals, made UHS a major behavioral-health operator with more than 300 facilities.

shieldingDetail.d: Each Class C share carries 100 votes. In the 2025 proxy Miller held all 661,688 Class C shares and 78.5% of Class A, for 87.8% of the general voting power.
Some of his shares are held through three LLCs and three 2024 grantor retained annuity trusts (GRATs) for his children.
His son Marc D. Miller became CEO in January 2021, and Alan stayed on as executive chairman.
In 2020 UHS agreed to a $122M settlement with the DOJ over billing for medically unnecessary behavioral-health services from 2006 to 2018.

name: John Malone
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1941 in Milford, Connecticut. He earned degrees from Yale, Johns Hopkins (including a PhD in operations research) and NYU, then worked in economic planning at Bell Labs, at McKinsey, and running General Instrument's Jerrold Electronics unit. He started out as an engineer-economist, not a man of inherited wealth.
breakthrough: Bob Magness hired him at Tele-Communications Inc. (TCI), and he became CEO in 1973 at 32. By 1982 he had made it the largest US cable company through debt-financed acquisitions. He spun off Liberty Media in 1991, and in 1999 sold TCI to AT&T for $32B in stock plus $16B of assumed debt.
shieldingStrategy: Known as the 'Cable Cowboy', he used tax-free spinoffs, tracking stocks and asset swaps instead of taxable sales. Super-voting Class B shares keep him in control across Liberty Media, Liberty Global and their spinoffs. He also holds about 2 million acres of land.

breakthroughDetail.d: TCI grew through acquisitions such as United Artists Entertainment (1991) and carried about $15B of debt by the mid-1990s, using cash flow rather than reported earnings as the measure.
Comcast and the TCI spinoff Liberty Media bought QVC together in February 1995. Liberty bought out Comcast's 56.5% in 2003 for $7.9B.
AT&T agreed to buy TCI in June 1998 and closed in March 1999. TCI's systems became AT&T Broadband, which Comcast bought in 2002.
An $11B swap with News Corp in 2008 gave Liberty 47.9% of DirecTV, Charlie Ergen's main rival. In 2013 Malone publicly urged that DISH and DirecTV merge.

shieldingDetail.d: Liberty has spun off Liberty Global, Discovery, Starz, Liberty Broadband, the Atlanta Braves (2023) and SiriusXM (2024) instead of selling them in taxable deals.
Liberty issues stocks that track separate asset groups, such as Formula One, under one corporate parent.
Malone keeps voting control of Liberty Media through its Class B shares despite repeated restructurings.

shieldingDetail.t: Land as a store of value.
shieldingDetail.d: He was the largest private landowner in the US from 2011 to 2021, with about 2.2 million acres in Maine, Colorado, New Mexico and Wyoming.

sources.label: Broadcasting & Cable — DirecTV is outpacing Dish, and now comes Malone (2008)

name: Charlie Ergen
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1953 in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the son of an Austrian nuclear physicist. He earned a Wake Forest MBA and worked as a financial analyst at Frito-Lay, then quit in 1978 and played poker and blackjack professionally for a time.
breakthrough: In 1980 he, his future wife Candy and Jim DeFranco put $60,000 into EchoSphere and sold C-band satellite dishes from a truck around Denver. EchoStar went public and launched its first satellite in 1995, and the DISH Network brand followed in 1996. DISH was spun off in 2008, and the two were recombined under EchoStar at the end of 2023.
shieldingStrategy: Controls EchoStar as its 'controlling shareholder' through Class B shares carrying ten votes each, about 90% of the voting power. He spent about a decade buying wireless spectrum and sold much of it in 2025 for cash and SpaceX stock. He and Candy are Giving Pledge signers.

breakthroughDetail.d: EchoSphere began in 1980 with $60,000 and sold satellite antennas door to door around Denver.
EchoStar I launched on December 28, 1995, and the DISH Network brand followed on March 4, 1996, moving the company from selling hardware to selling subscriptions.
In the late 1990s News Corp's planned tie-up with EchoStar fell apart. Ergen later said 'Malone got what he wanted' from that episode. Malone's Liberty went on to hold 47.9% of rival DirecTV.
In 2025 EchoStar agreed to sell spectrum to AT&T for $23B and to SpaceX for about $17B, half of it in SpaceX stock.

shieldingDetail.d: Each EchoStar Class B share carries ten votes, and Ergen is the company's controlling shareholder with roughly 90% of the voting power.
Cantey (Candy) Ergen, a co-founder in 1980, serves as a director and senior advisor.

shieldingDetail.t: Spectrum as a store of value.
shieldingDetail.d: Licenses bought over about a decade were later sold for roughly $40B, turning a declining pay-TV business into cash and SpaceX equity.
'Candy and Charlie Ergen' appear on the Giving Pledge list.

sources.label: SEC — EchoStar press release on SpaceX spectrum sale (Sept 2025)
Broadcasting & Cable — Book dishes on Malone, Ergen, Murdoch

name: Tyrone D. Taborn
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure, and this is a low-confidence estimate at the bottom of the tier. It rests on his roughly 40 years of private ownership of Career Communications Group, which business-data aggregators estimate at about $4-7M in annual revenue and HistoryMakers calls a 'multimillion-dollar' company, plus the BEYA conference franchise. No sale, valuation or real-estate figure is public.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Los Angeles in an African American and Latino household (HistoryMakers gives his birth as Chicago, 1959). He graduated from Cornell, where he was a Telluride Association scholar, also holds a BS from Johns Hopkins, and in 1978 was the first LBJ Congressional Intern, in Rep. Julian Dixon's office.
breakthrough: In the mid-1980s (company materials give both 1985 and 1986) he founded Career Communications Group in Baltimore to publish US Black Engineer, later US Black Engineer & Information Technology. With Morgan State engineering dean Eugene DeLoatch he co-founded the Black Engineer of the Year Awards, first held at Morgan State in February 1987. BEYA grew into a STEM conference with 100+ recruiting companies and more than 10,000 attendees.
shieldingStrategy: Kept CCG private and diversified it from one magazine into a set of titles (Hispanic Engineer, Women of Color) and events, sponsored by corporations and defense contractors. He plans to step down as publisher in 2028 and become board chairman, and family member Ty Oliver Taborn is general counsel.

breakthroughDetail.d: US Black Engineer profiled Black engineers and technologists whose work was 'too often missing from mainstream publications'. CCG has digitized back issues to 1984.
The first Black Engineer of the Year Awards were held at Morgan State in February 1987, during National Engineers Week, with Dr. John Slaughter as the first honoree.

BEYA is co-hosted by CCG, the Council of Engineering Deans of the HBCUs, and Lockheed Martin, which by 2011 had co-hosted for more than a decade. Boeing, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and IBM also recruit there.
An early report to Mobil's CEO led him to write to other Fortune 500 heads endorsing the program, which helped bring in corporate sponsors.

shieldingDetail.d: CCG has stayed privately held under Taborn since its founding and publishes no financials.
Revenue comes from several magazines and conferences, BEYA and the Women of Color STEM Conference, plus digital platforms such as STEM City USA, rather than a single title.
Taborn will step down as publisher in 2028 and remain chairman of the board while a new publisher is recruited.
In 2025 Taborn said some government agencies and corporate employers were reconsidering BEYA participation amid the backlash against DEI programs.

sources.label: St. Louis American — BEYA is where corporate America meets Black talent (2011)
USBE — Making the promise of BEYA: meet a first-ever winner
Baltimore Times/BmoreNews — A digital freedom fighter at 40
Hispanic Engineer — Taborn to step down as publisher in 2028
USBE — BEYA faces challenges amid DEI backlash

name: Ted Turner
humbleBeginnings: Born in Cincinnati in 1938, the son of billboard owner Robert Edward Turner II. After his father's suicide in March 1963, Turner took over the family's Turner Advertising Company at 24.
breakthrough: In 1970 he merged the billboard firm with Rice Broadcasting, gaining Atlanta UHF station WTCG, and in December 1976 put it on satellite as the first 'SuperStation' (later WTBS). He bought the Atlanta Braves (1976) to supply programming, launched CNN as the first 24-hour news network in June 1980, and sold Turner Broadcasting to Time Warner in 1996.
shieldingStrategy: When the 1986 MGM deal left him heavily in debt, he let a TCI-led group of cable operators buy 37% of TBS in 1987 rather than lose the company. He later swapped TBS for Time Warner stock (1996). That concentration cost him billions when AOL Time Warner shares collapsed, and he moved much of what remained into about 2 million acres of land and large gifts.

breakthroughDetail.d: Merged Turner Advertising with Rice Broadcasting in 1970, gaining WTCG. In December 1976 it began beaming nationwide by satellite as the SuperStation (WTBS).
Bought the Atlanta Braves in 1976 and the NBA's Atlanta Hawks in 1977, which gave the SuperStation live sports to fill its schedule.
Launched Cable News Network in June 1980 as the first 24-hour live news channel. TNT (1988) and Cartoon Network (1992) followed.
Bought MGM/UA from Kirk Kerkorian in 1986 for about $1.4–1.5B, sold the studio back and kept the pre-1986 MGM film library, the base for TNT and Turner Classic Movies.

shieldingDetail.d: In 1987, 31 cable operators led by TCI paid nearly $565M for 37% of TBS. Turner's stake fell from about 80% to 43%, and John Malone, HBO's Michael Fuchs and Warner Cable's Jim Gray joined the board.
Time Warner bought TBS in 1996 for stock (Forbes: $7.3B; Encyclopedia.com: $7.6B). Turner's fortune became Time Warner shares, and he estimated his losses at $7B after the 2001 AOL merger.

shieldingDetail.t: Land as a store of value.
shieldingDetail.d: Through Turner Enterprises he held about 2 million acres and the largest private bison herd. He was the largest private US landowner until John Malone passed him in 2011.

Pledged $1B to the UN in September 1997, paid at about $100M a year for 10 years through the new United Nations Foundation. He signed the Giving Pledge in 2010 and also funded the Turner Foundation (1990) and the Nuclear Threat Initiative (2001).

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Atlanta Braves owners and executives

name: Sheldon Adelson
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1933 in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, the son of a taxi driver and a mother who ran a knitting shop. At 10 he borrowed $200 from an uncle to start selling newspapers.
breakthrough: His Interface Group started COMDEX in Las Vegas in 1979, and it became one of the world's largest computer trade shows. He bought the Sands Hotel in 1988–89, replaced it with The Venetian (1999), and after Macau opened its casino market in 2002 built Sands Macao (2004) and Singapore's Marina Bay Sands (2010).
shieldingStrategy: He turned a trade show into a casino empire by selling COMDEX to SoftBank in 1995 for about $860M, of which he netted more than $500M. He kept control of Las Vegas Sands after its 2004 IPO, and at his death his family held about 58% through trusts. The fortune was concentrated: he lost about $4B in 2008 alone.

breakthroughDetail.d: The Interface Group (Adelson and Richard Katzeff) held the first COMDEX at the MGM Grand in December 1979 with 167 exhibitors. Attendance peaked at 225,000 in 1996.
Bought the Sands for $110M in 1988, demolished it, and opened The Venetian in May 1999 at a cost of about $1.5B.

LVS won a 2002 Macau concession with Galaxy Entertainment. When the partnership broke down, Macau created sub-concessions so each could operate separately. Sands Macao opened in May 2004 as the territory's first Las Vegas-style casino.
Marina Bay Sands opened in 2010 at about $5.5–5.6B, then the most expensive casino resort ever built.

shieldingDetail.t: Cash out of the first business.
shieldingDetail.d: Sold COMDEX to SoftBank in 1995 for about $860M. His share of more than $500M funded the casino build-out.

shieldingDetail.t: Family trusts over a listed company.
shieldingDetail.d: LVS went public in December 2004. At his death the Adelson family controlled about 58% of it through various trusts, and it still holds about 54%.
Sands China was listed in Hong Kong in 2009, raising capital for Macau while LVS kept majority control.
Because his wealth was almost all LVS stock, his net worth fell about 93% to roughly $2B by 2009 before rebounding to $37.2B by 2013.

sources.label: CDC Gaming Reports — Sheldon Adelson dies at 87
Asia Times — Macau mega-casino born of a broken marriage

name: Thomas F. Frist Jr.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Nashville in 1938, the son of internist Dr. Thomas F. Frist Sr., who founded Park View Hospital in 1960. He earned a BA at Vanderbilt and an MD at Washington University, then served as a US Air Force flight surgeon.
breakthrough: In 1968 he co-founded Hospital Corporation of America with his father and Jack C. Massey, starting from Park View. HCA went public in 1969 with 11 hospitals and had 349 by the end of 1981, making it the template for investor-owned hospital chains.
shieldingStrategy: He has taken HCA private twice, through a $5.1B management buyout he led in 1988 and the $33B buyout in 2006 alongside KKR, Bain Capital and Merrill Lynch, and taken it public again each time. The family's roughly 32% stake now sits in a listed company where he has no executive role and two sons are directors.

breakthroughDetail.d: HCA started in 1968 from Frist Sr.'s Park View Hospital. It went public in 1969 with 11 hospitals and ended that year with 26 hospitals and 3,000 beds.
By the end of 1981 HCA operated 349 hospitals with more than 49,000 beds. In 1987 it spun off 104 hospitals as HealthTrust.

HCA merged with Columbia Hospital Corp. in 1994. When Rick Scott was forced out in 1997 amid a federal fraud investigation, Frist returned as chairman and CEO. The government case ultimately brought in more than $2B in fines and penalties by 2003.

shieldingDetail.d: Frist led a $5.1B leveraged buyout that took HCA private, and it listed again in 1992.
He joined KKR, Bain Capital and Merrill Lynch Global Private Equity in the $33B buyout (closed November 17, 2006), then the largest LBO in history and bigger than RJR Nabisco.
The March 2011 IPO, then the largest private-equity-backed US IPO, raised about $3.8B while the sponsors and Frist kept control. Forbes puts the family's stake at about 32%.
The Frist Foundation helped found Nashville's Frist Art Museum. His sons Thomas Frist III and William Frist sit on HCA's board.

sources.label: Bass, Berry & Sims — HCA: from public company to private company, and back again

name: Frederick W. Smith
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1944 in Marks, Mississippi. His father founded the Toddle House restaurant chain and Dixie Greyhound Lines and left money in a trust that paid out when Fred turned 21. He studied economics at Yale, then served as a Marine platoon leader and forward air controller in Vietnam, earning the Silver Star, the Bronze Star and two Purple Hearts.
breakthrough: He built on an idea from a 1965 Yale paper: fly every package through a single hub overnight. After buying control of Arkansas Aviation Sales, he founded Federal Express in 1971 and launched it from Memphis on April 17, 1973, with 14 Dassault Falcon jets serving 25 cities. FedEx reached $1B in revenue by 1983.
shieldingStrategy: He put in about $4M of his inheritance and raised one of the largest venture rounds of its time, about $72M led by New Court Securities from General Dynamics, Prudential, Allstate, Chase Manhattan and Citibank, at the cost of heavy dilution. Early on he kept about 15% of the company, and he ran it as CEO for 50 years until 2022.

breakthroughDetail.d: Overnight service began April 17, 1973, with 14 Falcon 20s linking 25 cities through the central Memphis hub.

FedEx lost $29M in its first 26 months, and investors put in another $11M at steep terms. By Smith's own story, he flew the company's last $5,000 to Las Vegas and won $27,000 at blackjack to cover fuel.
Bought Flying Tiger Line (1988, about $880M) for international routes, Caliber System/RPS (1998) for ground delivery, Kinko's (2004, $2.4B) and TNT Express (deal announced 2015).

shieldingDetail.d: Memphis magazine: a total of $72M was secured, including money from General Dynamics, Prudential, Allstate, Chase Manhattan and Citibank, which it called the largest venture raise in US business history up to then.
Around the 1978 IPO (about 1M shares at $24), Memphis magazine put Smith's stake at about 15%. He stayed CEO until June 2022, when Raj Subramaniam took over, and remained executive chairman.
His sisters sued over family-trust shares he had pledged to keep FedEx alive, and he settled out of court in 1979 once the company was profitable.
Gave a record $65M to the Marine Corps Scholarship Foundation in 2022.

sources.label: Memphis magazine — Federal Express: the million-dollar dream machine

name: Sam Walton
humbleBeginnings: Born in Kingfisher, Oklahoma, in 1918. He joined JCPenney as a management trainee in 1940 at $75 a month. After Army service he bought a Ben Franklin variety-store franchise in Newport, Arkansas, in 1945 with $5,000 of savings and a $20,000 loan from his father-in-law, Leland Robson.
breakthrough: Lost the Newport lease, restarted in Bentonville in 1950, and opened the first Walmart in Rogers, Arkansas, on July 2, 1962. Walmart went public on October 1, 1970 at $16.50 a share, opened Sam's Club in 1983, and had 1,960 Walmart stores and about $50B in annual sales when he died in 1992.
shieldingStrategy: In 1953, on Leland Robson's advice, he put the business into Walton Enterprises, a family partnership in which each of his four children owned 20%. That vehicle, now an LLC and the family office, is still Walmart's largest shareholder.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built the Newport Ben Franklin store from $80,000 to $225,000 in sales in three years, then lost the lease and sold the store for $50,000. He reopened on the Bentonville square on May 9, 1950.
Opened the first Walmart in Rogers, Arkansas, on July 2, 1962. With his brother Bud he already ran 16 stores across three states that year, and the chain grew from 190 stores in 1977 to 800 in 1985.
Wal-Mart incorporated in October 1969, sold stock to the public on October 1, 1970 at $16.50 a share, and listed on the NYSE in 1972 with 51 stores and $78M in sales.
Launched Sam's Club in Midwest City, Oklahoma, in 1983 and the first Supercenter in Washington, Missouri, in 1988.

shieldingDetail.d: Walton Enterprises (1953) made Sam, Helen and the four children partners: the parents jointly held 20% and each child 20%, so later growth accrued to the children.
The 1970 offering sold only a minority, and the family vehicle remains Walmart's largest holder (37.3% via Walton Enterprises).
Sam and Helen set up the Walton Family Foundation in 1987, on Walmart's 25th anniversary.

sources.label: Oklahoma Historical Society: Walton, Samuel Moore

name: Rob Walton
humbleBeginnings: Eldest son of Sam Walton, born in Tulsa in 1944. He earned a law degree from Columbia in 1969 and practised at Conner & Winters in Tulsa, where he did legal work on Walmart's 1970 IPO.
breakthrough: Joined Walmart as a senior vice president in 1978, became vice chairman in 1982 and chairman on April 7, 1992, two days after his father died. He chaired the company until 2015, and in 2022 led the $4.65B purchase of the Denver Broncos, a record for a sports team at the time.
shieldingStrategy: His wealth sits mostly in Walmart shares held through Walton Enterprises, which he helped structure as a lawyer, and the Walton Family Holdings Trust. He passed control of the Broncos to his son-in-law Greg Penner in 2023 and left Walmart's board in 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: At Conner & Winters he helped organize the family's Walmart holdings into Walton Enterprises and did legal work on the October 1970 IPO.
Senior vice president in 1978, vice chairman in 1982, then chairman from April 1992 until 2015; Greg Penner, his son-in-law, succeeded him as chair.
His group agreed to buy the Denver Broncos on June 7, 2022 for $4.65B; the NFL approved it in August 2022. Partners include Penner, Condoleezza Rice, Mellody Hobson and Lewis Hamilton.

shieldingDetail.d: Walton Enterprises, now an LLC, holds 37.3% of Walmart and is the family's main vehicle.
In March 2020 the family moved 14% of Walmart's shares from Walton Enterprises into the Walton Family Holdings Trust (created 2015) without changing their total ownership.
The Waltons together own about 45% of Walmart, enough for effective control without a dual-class structure.
Penner took over the Walmart chair in 2015 and controlling ownership of the Broncos in 2023.

name: Richard M. Schulze
humbleBeginnings: Born in Saint Paul in 1941, he finished high school, served in the Minnesota Air National Guard and sold electronics components. In 1966 he mortgaged his home to open Sound of Music, a car- and home-audio store.
breakthrough: After a tornado destroyed one store, a 'tornado sale' of heavily discounted stock showed him the pull of selection and low prices. He renamed the chain Best Buy around 1983, moved to big-box superstores with salaried, non-commission staff, and reached $5B in sales and 155 stores by 1995.
shieldingStrategy: He stayed Best Buy's largest individual shareholder (about 5% today) rather than selling out. He resigned as chairman in 2012 after an audit-committee review of how he handled a complaint about the CEO, failed to take the company private, and returned as chairman emeritus in 2013. He gives through the family foundation he formed in 2002.

breakthroughDetail.d: Opened Sound of Music in 1966, funded by a mortgage on his home.
A tornado destroyed one store; the clearance sale that followed pointed him to large selection and low prices, and the chain became Best Buy around 1983 with 18,000 sq ft superstores.
Dropped commission selling and added software, music, movies and computers; CEO from 1983 to 2002.

shieldingDetail.d: Owned about 20% in 2012 and remains the largest individual shareholder at about 5% (Forbes).

Stepped down as chairman in May 2012 after the board's review, offered to take Best Buy private in August 2012, saw the financing fall through by February 2013, and came back as chairman emeritus in March 2013.
The Richard M. Schulze Family Foundation (2002) carries his $1B giving pledge, including $50M to the University of St. Thomas (2000) and $49M to the Mayo Clinic (2006).

name: Arthur Blank
humbleBeginnings: Born in Flushing, Queens, in 1942 to a pharmacist father. After Babson College he worked as an accountant at Arthur Young, then rose through Daylin's retail units to finance VP at Handy Dan Home Improvement Centers under Bernie Marcus.
breakthrough: Fired with Marcus from Handy Dan in 1978 in a corporate power struggle, he co-founded The Home Depot that year with Ken Langone's financing; the first two stores opened in Atlanta on June 22, 1979. He was president for 19 years, succeeded Marcus as CEO, and retired as co-chairman in 2001.
shieldingStrategy: He moved his Home Depot wealth into Atlanta sports: the Falcons (bought 2002 for $545M), Atlanta United and the shared Mercedes-Benz Stadium. He gives through the Arthur M. Blank Family Foundation and signed the Giving Pledge in 2012.

breakthroughDetail.d: Blank and Marcus were fired from Handy Dan in 1978 and started The Home Depot the same year with merchandiser Pat Farrah and banker Ken Langone.
The first two stores opened June 22, 1979 in former Treasure Island sites in Atlanta; the company listed on Nasdaq in 1981 and the NYSE in 1984.
Bought the Falcons in February 2002 for $545M, founded Atlanta United (MLS, 2017), and later added TGL golf and NWSL teams.

shieldingDetail.d: Chairs the Arthur M. Blank Family Foundation; gifts include $200M to Children's Healthcare of Atlanta.
Signed in 2012, committing to give away most of his wealth.
Swapped part of a single-stock fortune for team franchises, which have appreciated many times over (Forbes values his Falcons stake at $6.7B).

name: Bernie Marcus
humbleBeginnings: Born in Newark in 1929 to Russian Jewish immigrants. Unable to afford Harvard Medical School, he took a pharmacy degree at Rutgers and worked as a pharmacist before moving into retail with Odell and then Daylin.
breakthrough: Became CEO of Daylin's Handy Dan Improvement Centers, was fired in April 1978, and co-founded The Home Depot that year with Arthur Blank, Ken Langone and Pat Farrah. He was CEO from 1978 to 1997 and chairman until 2002, building the world's largest home-improvement retailer.
shieldingStrategy: Signed the Giving Pledge with his wife Billi in 2010, pledging 90% of his fortune, and gave close to $2B through the Marcus Foundation, including $250M to build the Georgia Aquarium. He retired from the board in 2002 at the mandatory age of 72.

breakthroughDetail.d: Worked at Odell (1968) and Daylin (1970) before running Handy Dan.

breakthroughDetail.t: A firing that founded a company.
breakthroughDetail.d: Fired from Handy Dan in April 1978, he started The Home Depot with Blank, Langone and Farrah; the first two Atlanta stores opened June 22, 1979.
CEO 1978-1997 and chairman 1978-2002; GE veteran Bob Nardelli became CEO in 2000 and chairman in 2002.

shieldingDetail.d: Pledged 90% of his fortune in 2010 with Billi Marcus.
Gave close to $2B in his lifetime, including $250M for the Georgia Aquarium and $75M to Piedmont Healthcare.
Retired from Home Depot's board in 2002 under its age-72 rule.

name: Ken Langone
humbleBeginnings: Born in Roslyn Heights, New York, in 1935 to a plumber and a cafeteria worker, the grandson of Italian immigrants. He worked construction and earned degrees from Bucknell and an MBA from NYU Stern.
breakthrough: At R.W. Pressprich in 1968 he persuaded Ross Perot to let the firm take Electronic Data Systems public, and became Pressprich's president in 1969. He founded Invemed in 1974 and in 1978 raised the money that launched The Home Depot.
shieldingStrategy: Kept his Home Depot founders' stake for decades ('I got rich by never selling') and runs his business through his private firm, Invemed. He gives through large named gifts, including $200M that renamed NYU's medical center NYU Langone, and is a Giving Pledge signatory.

breakthroughDetail.d: In 1968 he won Ross Perot's mandate for Pressprich to take EDS public; Pressprich named him president the next year.
Founded Invemed Associates in 1974 and organized the starting capital for Marcus and Blank in 1978; he was a director from 1978 and lead director by 2002.
While a director of both GE and Home Depot he offered Bob Nardelli the Home Depot job minutes after Jack Welch told Nardelli he would not be GE's next CEO (2000).
Sat on the NYSE board and its compensation committee (1999-2003) when Richard Grasso's $139.5M pay package was approved; a 2004 lawsuit naming him over that pay was dismissed in 2008.

shieldingDetail.d: Forbes records his stance of holding Home Depot shares long term; he also holds stakes in Eli Lilly and Yum! Brands.
Invemed, his own investment bank and venture firm, keeps his dealmaking outside public-company disclosure.
Gave $200M to NYU's medical center (renamed NYU Langone) and $100M toward free tuition at its medical school (2018); Giving Pledge signatory.

name: Howard Schultz
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in public housing in Canarsie, Brooklyn, and was the first in his family to graduate from college (Northern Michigan University, 1975). He sold Xerox machines and then ran U.S. sales for the Swedish housewares maker Hammarplast.
breakthrough: Joined Starbucks, then a Seattle bean roaster founded in 1971 by Jerry Baldwin, Zev Siegl and Gordon Bowker, as director of retail operations and marketing in 1982. When the owners rejected his espresso-bar idea he left and opened Il Giornale in 1986. In 1987 Il Giornale bought the Starbucks business for $3.8M, and he grew it from 11 stores to more than 35,000.
shieldingStrategy: He did not found Starbucks: he bought it in 1987 with money from local investors, after beating off an investor's attempt to buy the company and keep him on only as a manager. He served three terms as CEO, invests through Maveron (co-founded 1998) and gives through the Schultz Family Foundation.

breakthroughDetail.d: Raised about $400,000 for Il Giornale in 1986, pitching 242 potential investors; Starbucks itself put in $150,000.
In 1987 Il Giornale bought Starbucks for $3.8M and took its name. After an investor tried to buy Starbucks out from under him, other backers rallied to fund the deal.
Starbucks listed in June 1992 with 140 outlets and $73.5M in revenue; Schultz was CEO 1986-2000, 2008-2017 and interim CEO 2022-2023.

In 1998 Starbucks and Johnson Development Corp. formed Urban Coffee Opportunities, a 50/50 venture that opened more than 100 stores in neighborhoods such as Harlem, Bronzeville and Crenshaw; Starbucks bought Johnson's half in October 2010.

shieldingDetail.d: His control came from buying the company with outside investors' money in 1987, not from founding it.
Co-founded Maveron with Dan Levitan in 1998; it backed eBay, Shutterfly and Zulily.
Sold the SuperSonics and Storm in 2006 for $350M to Clay Bennett's Oklahoma City group.
Co-founded the Schultz Family Foundation in 1996 to fund youth employment and veterans' programs.

sources.label: FoodIngredientsFirst: Starbucks acquires remaining interest in Urban Coffee Opportunities (2010)
Starbucks: nominates Brewer, Knudstorp and Nadella to its board (2017)

name: Estée Lauder
peakWealth: Company valued at >$2B at its 1995 IPO
wealthNote: No personal net-worth figure appears in the sources opened. The company was valued at more than $2B when it listed in 1995 with the family keeping control, and the Lauder family's wealth was later estimated at about $33B (2022). The tier rests on that family stake.
humbleBeginnings: Born Josephine Esther Mentzer in Corona, Queens, in 1908 to Hungarian and Czech immigrant parents. She began by selling skin creams made from her chemist uncle John Schotz's formulas to women in Manhattan beauty salons.
breakthrough: Founded the company with her husband Joseph Lauder in 1946. In 1948 she persuaded Saks Fifth Avenue to carry the line, and Youth-Dew (1953) persuaded women to buy perfume for themselves, multiplying sales. Clinique, Aramis and, later, acquired brands such as M.A.C followed.
shieldingStrategy: The company stayed family-owned for nearly 50 years, by her death the largest privately held cosmetics company in the world. When it listed in November 1995, a dual-class structure kept control with the family, which today holds about 38% of the equity and 86% of the votes.

breakthroughDetail.d: Sold her uncle's creams directly in beauty salons before founding Estée Lauder Cosmetics at 501 Madison Avenue in 1946.
Won a Saks Fifth Avenue counter in 1948, moving from salons into department stores.
Pioneered free samples and gift-with-purchase promotions, which became industry practice.
Launched in 1953; it sold 50,000 bottles in its first year and 150 million by 1984.

shieldingDetail.d: Reinvested profits and stayed private until 1995.
Listed on the NYSE on November 16, 1995 at $26 a share; the family today holds about 38% of the equity and 86% of the votes.
Son Leonard led the company after her; grandson William P. Lauder is chairman.

sources.label: PBS: They Made America, Estée Lauder
Al Jazeera: Makeup icon Estée Lauder dies (2004)

name: Tim Cook
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Robertsdale, Alabama, the son of a shipyard worker and a pharmacy employee, and graduated salutatorian of his high school in 1978. He studied industrial engineering at Auburn and later earned a Duke MBA while working at IBM.
breakthrough: Steve Jobs hired him from Compaq in 1998 to run Apple's worldwide operations. He closed factories, cut inventory from months to days and locked up long-term flash-memory supply, then succeeded Jobs as CEO in August 2011. Apple's market value rose from about $350B to $4T on his watch, and on September 1, 2026 he handed the CEO job to John Ternus and became executive chairman.
shieldingStrategy: He never founded or controlled Apple: his fortune is a sub-1% stake built from restricted stock units and has been partly sold down over time. He has said he plans to give his fortune to charity.

breakthroughDetail.d: Joined from Compaq in 1998 as SVP of worldwide operations after 12 years at IBM. He closed Apple's factories, cut inventory and secured long-term flash-memory deals that fed the iPod nano, iPhone and iPad.

In 2014 Apple bought Beats Electronics for $3B ($2.6B upfront plus about $400M vesting over time), its largest acquisition, and hired co-founders Dr. Dre and Jimmy Iovine. Beats Music became the base for Apple Music in 2015.
Apple is TSMC's largest customer (about 26% of its 2021 revenue), and in December 2022 Cook said Apple was 'proud to become the site's largest customer' at TSMC's new Arizona fabs.

breakthroughDetail.t: Search and AI ties to Google.
breakthroughDetail.d: Google pays Apple billions a year to be Safari's default search engine, a deal at the center of the DOJ antitrust case that a 2025 remedy ruling allowed to continue. In January 2026 the two companies said Gemini models will underpin Apple's next-generation foundation models and Siri.

shieldingDetail.d: His pay is mostly restricted stock tied to Apple's shareholder return. His FY2025 compensation was $74.3M, including $57.5M in stock awards, and as executive chairman his FY2027 target is $47M.
Forbes reports he owns more than 3 million Apple shares and has sold over $1B of stock during his tenure. In August 2021 alone he sold about $750M worth.
In March 2015 he announced plans to donate his fortune to charity. He is not listed as a controlling holder and has no dual-class or family-holding structure.

sources.label: Apple Newsroom — Tim Cook to become executive chairman, John Ternus to become CEO (Apr 2026)
Taipei Times — Apple to be TSMC US fab top customer (Dec 2022)
Google — Joint statement from Google and Apple (Jan 12, 2026)

name: John Ternus
wealthNote: No published net worth. He was not a named executive officer in Apple's proxies before becoming CEO, so his pay as SVP of hardware engineering was never disclosed. Bloomberg (via 9to5Mac) says Apple executives at that level typically earn about $25M a year including stock. Five years as SVP (2021–26) at that rate is roughly $125M before tax, and he was a VP from 2013. How much he kept after taxes and sales is unknown, so the conservative tier is used. He could plausibly exceed $100M. His CEO package ($3M salary plus a $55M equity target for FY2027) is mostly unvested.
humbleBeginnings: Born in California in 1975, he studied mechanical engineering at the University of Pennsylvania (BS 1997), where he swam on the varsity team. He then designed virtual-reality headsets as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.
breakthrough: He joined Apple's product design team in 2001, starting on the Cinema Display. He rose to VP of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021, overseeing the iPad, AirPods, iPhone and the Mac's move from Intel to Apple silicon. Apple named him CEO in April 2026, effective September 1, 2026, and he also joined the board.
shieldingStrategy: A career employee with no founder stake. His wealth is Apple restricted stock, and his CEO equity is 75% performance-based RSUs tied to Apple's shareholder return relative to the S&P 500.

breakthroughDetail.d: Joined in 2001 to work on the Apple Cinema Display, became VP of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021. Apple says he worked under Steve Jobs and was mentored by Tim Cook.
From 2020 he oversaw moving the Mac from Intel to Apple-designed chips. That year he also took over iPhone hardware.
Apple credits him with work on the iPad and AirPods lines, multiple iPhone generations (including iPhone 17, 17 Pro and iPhone Air), the Mac (including MacBook Neo) and Apple Watch.
The board approved the succession unanimously, and Cook moved to executive chairman.

shieldingDetail.d: His CEO package is a $3M salary plus a $55M equity target for FY2027. Three-quarters is performance RSUs tied to relative TSR, and the time-based quarter vests 12.5% every six months over four years. He also got a $2.5M prorated grant for FY2026.
His SVP pay was never disclosed in Apple's proxy. That is typical for non-named officers and keeps an executive's accumulated wealth out of public view.

sources.label: Apple Newsroom — Tim Cook to become executive chairman, John Ternus to become CEO (Apr 2026)
MacRumors — What Apple is paying John Ternus (Sep 2026)
